Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, this petition is hereby certified correct as to form and content. It contains 28 signatures but represents over 3,000 signatures which I have received on behalf of people who are opposed to the importation of the killer cards.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents of central British Columbia who are dedicated in their opposition to the plan to divert part of the North Thompson River in an effort to sell the water in the San Diego, California area.
The petitioners are of the opinion that the North America free trade agreement will facilitate this. This concerns them obviously and they ask that the government take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that Canadian waters will never be diverted into the United States.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ELIMINATION OF VIOLENCE IN OUR SOCIETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to table a petition from residents of Val d'Or, Sullivan, Barraute, La Motte, Saint-Dominique-du-Rosaire, Saint-Felix, Villemontel, Senneterre and the Senior Citizens Club of Val-Senneville, all in the riding of Abitibi. Your petitioners say that films depicting violence on television are dangerous and therefore unacceptable because they act as a stimulus for violent behaviour.
The petition also says that all toys that incite children to play violent games are unacceptable and their manufacture should be banned. It is also pointed out that the freedom of the press should be restricted when reporting on acts of violence, and that the repeated broadcasting of news about acts of violence on television, on all channels and on radio may act as a stimulus for similar violent behaviour.
Therefore your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to pass the appropriate legislation in order to eliminate violence in our society and thus protect our children and give all citizens a better quality of life.

Mr. Speaker, I have several thousand signatures to present today on petitions. This will make over 1,400,000 signatures we have received from across Canada from people who are in support of the parents of Nina de Villiers. They feel that many people in Canada are vulnerable with little protection under the current criminal justice system, the Criminal Code, and that women, children and disabled persons are particularly at risk.
These signatures request that Parliament recognize crimes of violence against the person as serious and abhorrent to society. They ask the government to amend the Criminal Code of Canada, the Bail Reform Act, 1972, and the Parole Act accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to present this petition on behalf of Canadians from Winnipeg, the maritimes and other areas. Apparently meningococcal disease has taken many lives of children in Canada. A test kit that can detect all types of this disease in its early stages now exists.
These petitioners pray that Parliament call upon the Department of National Health and Welfare to ensure that this test kit is fully developed so that our citizens may fully benefit from it.

Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions to present this morning. The first comes from people in my constituency who are most concerned about the question of child poverty in this country.
February 23, 1993

In their petition they note that the House of Commons unanimously passed a motion in 1989 expressing its concern for the more than one million Canadian children currently living in poverty. They also note that the House of Commons established the goal of eliminating poverty among Canadian children by the year 2000.
The petition indicates some of the continuing realities of poverty for children in Canada. It concludes with the petitioners who have signed it praying and calling upon Parliament to take the actions necessary to reaffirm that 1989 commitment to seek the elimination of poverty among children in Canada by the year 2000 and to develop a plan for the implementation of this commitment.

Mr. Speaker, the second petition is from people in the town of Essex in my constituency who organized a series of events including a petition last year to promote pride in being Canadian.
They indicate in this petition that they believe it is appropriate to encourage all Canadians to take pride in a united, strong and independent Canada. They suggest that through the "Proud to be a Canadian" project brought forward by Kinsmen and Kinette clubs throughout Canada an opportunity should be provided for Canadians to nurture a strong relationship with our heritage and our flag, to encourage stronger ties among all Canadians for the further advancement of Canada as a leader in world circles, and to promote our tremendous pride in being Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I too have pleasure in presenting a petition from my riding that reminds the House that we unanimously passed a resolution on November 24, 1989 expressing concern for the more than one million Canadian children living in poverty and setting the goal of eliminating child poverty by the year 2000.
The petition reminds us all that child poverty represents increasing costs in the health care system, the justice system, social welfare, school dropouts, loss of productivity and, more important, loss of human potential.
The United Nations convention includes a moral and legal obligation to do as the petition asks and to
Government Orders
implement plans to eliminate child poverty in the next seven years as we have said we would do.

Mr. Speaker, I too have two petitions reminding the House of the unanimous resolution of November 24, 1989 that the House express its concern for the more than one million Canadian children currently living in poverty and resolve to achieve the goal of eliminating poverty among Canadian children by the year 2000.
The petitioners remind the House of the enormous cost for Canada of allowing unalleviated this poverty to continue. They ask us to work toward achieving the goal of eliminating child poverty by the year 2000.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
that Bill C-92, an act to amend the Income Ikx Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Income Ikx Conventions Interpretation Act, the Ikx Rebate Discounting Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and certain related acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Economics envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of presenting for consideration to the House second reading of Bill C-92, a bill that proposes to amend the Income Ikx Act and various other acts.

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
This bill will implement a number of important measures that were first announced in the February 1992 budget. It delivers on a key undertaking of this government to cut spending so that we can cut taxes and foster growth and competitiveness. As well, the bill includes a number of technical amendments to the Income Tax Act.
I see my hon. friend across the way grinning because it seems like we never stop introducing and implementing technical amendments. While this package is rather comprehensive in that light we hope that it will remove quite a backlog that has accumulated over time.
The budget measures in many respects reflect the views of Canadians in the very comprehensive cross-Canada consultation process that I conducted prior to the February 1992 budget. In the course of that the message that I received very loud and clear was the fact that Canadians expect their governments to cut spending. They want the deficit controlled. They want measures taken to stimulate growth and encourage job creation. They want to see investments made that will produce wealth and in a productive way stimulate and generate growth and wealth for the economy.
Most of all, they want a lower tax burden because Canadians believe that they have been overly burdened with the level of taxes. This bill reflects that and reflects those principles outlined in the budget of February 1992.
As well, the technical amendments contained in the bill reflect the constructive input which we have received from taxpayers and their advisers over the past few years. The aim of these amendments is to maintain and enhance the equity and efficiency of the tax system. This represents an important element of the tax system and our commitment to strengthen the Canadian economy by removing impediments and distortions caused by the tax system.
As I said, while this is a fairly large package it does remove a backlog that has accumulated for quite some time. Our hope is to proceed with this on a more regular basis so that we will not have to deal with such a large number of initiatives and perhaps will deal with it on a more frequent basis in a much more manageable way.
In outlining the measures in this bill I would like to begin with a description of some of the tax reductions
that are being proposed. First, Bill C-92 would give legislative approval to the 1 per cent reduction in the surtax on the personal income tax that came into effect on July 1, 1992.
As well, there is the additional one percentage point reduction that came into effect on January 1, 1993. With these measures announced in the budget, the surtax declines in two stages from 5 per cent of the basic federal tax to 3 per cent.
In this connection, all 14.6 million Canadian taxpayers will benefit from these reductions. For example, the single taxpayer earning $30,000 would receive a reduction of federal tax of $76 in 1993. A one income couple with two children and earnings of $50,000 would receive a reduction of $162 in federal tax this year.
These steps are expected to reduce federal revenues in this fiscal year, 1992-93, by some $500 million. The total impact over the period 1992-93 to 1996-97 is expected to amount to $6.6 billion. I should point out that these reductions are being covered by cutting expenditures elsewhere in government consistent with the theme of what we heard as we travelled across the country.
As well, these tax reductions reflect a central aspect of the government's philosophy on how best to foster growth. We believe that Canadians can make better and more productive use of their money than governments can. Our philosophy is that the more money we can leave in people's pockets the better it will be for our economy. That is a constant theme that we have followed and will continue to follow to the very best of our ability.
In addition a number of changes are implemented here for Canadian business. The goal of these initiatives is to assist companies in the manufacturing and processing sector as they restructure their operations and take advantage of the opportunities presented by the new age of globalization and the challenges presented by the increasing competitiveness in world markets.
The manufacturing and processing sector, as we are all aware, accounts for about one-fifth of Canada's domestic product. The economic health of this sector is therefore vital to the over-all health of the Canadian economy. It is also a sector that has perhaps been exposed more to international competition and adjustment in restructuring than any other sector.
February 23, 1993

All sectors of course have been exposed but this one has in a particular way been exposed. As a result of the exposure it is expected that the manufacturing and processing sector must become more productive and more competitive. In the course of that it means the challenge of producing more goods with fewer people.
That is an adjustment we have seen witnessed in the agricultural sector. We now see it happening in the manufacturing sector. That is part of the evolution of a vibrant world economy. Our goal and our aim is to assist in the process of facilitating that adjustment process. It is also to ensure that our Canadian industry is competitive, that it can compete in world markets, because so much of our vitality depends upon the export sector.
This exposure can only grow as trade and investment barriers continue to fall throughout the world and as technological advances make it possible for companies to have increasing flexibility as to where they locate their production facilities.
This does indeed provide challenges and opportunities for Canadian firms to expand and grow, building on their success to date and building upon our ability to compete. Currently 40 per cent of the manufacturing and processing output of these firms is exported. That clearly demonstrates the importance of the export market. It also forces a discipline on Canadian industry and governments to ensure that they have the appropriate structure, the appropriate financial environment and the appropriate investment environment in place so that companies engaged in this very important sector can extract the maximum of productivity and efficiency.
It is with this in mind that we propose to reduce the tax rate on income, the income tax on corporations derived from the manufacturing and processing, from 23 per cent to 21 per cent in two stages. The first decline takes effect on January 1, 1993. The second one is scheduled for January 1, 1994. The tax reduction complements two other measures announced in the budget. The first is a commitment to negotiate with other countries with respect to the deduction of withholding taxes. The second is an increase in the allowable capital cost allowance for manufacturing and processing equipment.
In that case we reduced effective budget night, February 25, the capital cost allowance. We increased it from
Government Orders
25 per cent to 30 per cent. When taken all together, the three corporate tax measures would mean that a Canadian manufacturing company not subject to the withholding tax would be subject to a significantly lower statutory tax rate in Canada than its competition in the U.S., 35 per cent versus 39 per cent, again demonstrating the thrust of this budget to improve the competitiveness for the Canadian sector.
For a company that is a subsidiary of the U.S. parent, total income and withholding tax would be less in Canada than it is in the United States.
We took these steps to provide incentives that would encourage investment and build a healthy economy and of course to create jobs, to secure the stability and the strength of those existing companies and to nurture and encourage other companies to become involved and take advantage of the newly emerging economy.
We know that from time to time we have to adjust our investment measures to ensure that they reflect the fiscal reality of the government, that they respond to economic conditions and that we get the best value for the taxpayers' dollars that are provided through these incentives.
To this end Bill C-92 proposes to target the lifetime exemption for capital gains toward more equity investment. In other words it will try to encourage more investment in firms that produce well, that generate jobs and generate economic activity.
The Income Tax Act therefore will be amended to no longer provide the $100,000 lifetime capital gains exemption on real estate purchased after February 1992 and to restrict it on real estate purchased before March 1992.
For the greater certainty of this particular measure, I would like to clarify some important points. First, this change does not apply to real estate used in active business. Second, it does not affect the $500,000 exemption for qualified small business shares and qualified farm property. Third, it does not affect the exemption on capital gains from the sale of principal residences and I think that is veiy important. The thrust of the lifetime capital gains exemption is left intact. What we are doing here is providing a measure which would hopefully encourage more investment in equity, more investment in productive enterprises that would generate jobs and generate growth.

Government Orders
The bill also proposes to modify the rules of the labour sponsored venture capital corporations, which are investment funds set up by labour organizations to purchase shares in small businesses. These changes include an increase in the maximum credit for investments in these funds from $700 to $1,000, an increase in the size of the company in which the funds may invest and a relaxation in the eligibility criteria for the fund sponsorship.
I should say that this too has been a very useful and encouraging kind of measure which brings ordinary workers more into the opportunity of investing in their own corporations.
There are some other measures I would like to refer to such as the home buyers' plan. As we have seen, economic growth has been strengthened by the home buyers' plan which was announced in the 1992 budget. This measure allows home buyers to withdraw up to $20,000 in existing funds from registered retirement savings plans and to use the money to finance the purchase of new or existing homes.
Where the home is being occupied as the buyer's principal residence, there is no tax on the withdrawal. The withdrawal is repayable to the home buyer's RRSP in equal instalments over a 15-year period.
Since this plan was announced, the response from Canadians has been impressive and so far there have been some 130,000 withdrawals under this plan. This initiative together with the reduced CMHC down payment requirement from 10 per cent to 5 per cent has helped in increasing housing starts in 1992 by some 7.7 per cent over 1991.
This has been an initiative that has been utilized. It has certainly helped people to get into homes. There is perhaps nothing that generates more economic spin-off than the home building industry. We not only have the activity of the building of the home, but indeed we have the spin-off in terms of equipping the home with furnishings and appliances. It does have a very positive impact in improving domestic demand. A one year extension of the plan was announced in the December economic statement and legislation to implement this extension will be introduced shortly.
Another change that was proposed in this legislation is to modify the tax system so that it treats common law
couples in the same way as married couples. The broader definition of spouse that is currently used in the Income Tax Act for provisions relating to pensions and other retirement plans will be extended for all other purposes under this act. Under this broader definition the term "spouses" will include both married and common law spouses.
I would like to now turn to some of the technical amendments of the Income Thx Act that we are proposing in Bill C-92. First of all we propose to reverse the ordering of the credit currently provided for the large corporations tax in the special Part VI tax on financial institutions against the corporate surtax and income tax. This will allow foreign parents of Canadian companies to obtain recognition abroad for a larger portion of the Canadian taxes for which they are liable and provide an added incentive for them to continue investing in the Canadian economy.
Second, we propose to amend the Income Ihx Act so that once the bill is enacted the government can collect a portion of taxes in cases where there is a dispute. This provision will apply only to disputed taxes of companies that are liable to the tax on large corporations. Individual taxpayers and small companies will not be required to pay over disputed taxes until a court has ultimately ruled on the question of liability of those taxes.
As well, we are proposing certain changes to the 21 year rule for trusts. These changes were initially announced on February 11, 1991. One measure will ensure that the 21 year period cannot be refreshed by transferring trust assets to new trusts. Other changes would ensure that capital gains consequences will be substantially the same whether individuals make a gift of property directly to their children or make the gift to a trust for the children's benefit.
In this connection there are a number of issues and misunderstandings that I would like to address because there has been, even on the floor of the House of Commons, some questions raised about this issue and some interpretations about it which are not correct. These misunderstandings essentially fall into three categories. First, it has been suggested that wealthy individuals are able to avoid taxes by setting up trusts. This is simply not the case. When property is transferred to a trust, any capital gains which have accrued on property must be recognized at that time.
February 23, 1993

Furthermore, trusts or their beneficiaries are subject to income tax each year on income generated in the trust just like any other taxpayer. Gains accruing while property is held in a trust are treated as accruing for the benefit of the trust beneficiaries, an approach which reflects the legal reality of these arrangements.
Second, it has been suggested that the distribution of trust property to beneficiaries within the 21 year period results in an unintended tax deferral. Again, this is simply incorrect. This is not the case. Such distributions are treated on a roll-over basis, recognizing that trust property is being held for the beneficiaries and should be treated in the same way as if it had been transferred directly to them. The 21 year rule was never intended to prevent this treatment of trust distributions.
Third, it has been suggested that substantial sums of tax revenues will be forgone as a result of these changes and this too is unfounded. Most trust property in the absence of these changes would have been distributed to beneficiaries before the end of the 21 year period and in such cases capital gains would be payable by the beneficiaries when the property was sold or ultimately on their death. The proposed changes will not alter this result.
I think this is very important because it is an important mechanism in terms of administering estates and administering people's holdings. Some may not have the capacity to do it on their own and so the set-up in the trust of this nature is very important.
There are a number of other technical measures which I do not intend to go into in detail. The explanatory notes provided by the department will clearly explain these measures. For hon. members who wish to become more familiar with these, I would suggest that they refer to the explanatory notes prepared by the Department of Finance. That includes the Net Income Stabilization Account program which was established in the Farm Income Protection Act; the disposition of capital property on death; the evaluation of employee stock options after death; the tax status of employees of the United Nations and agencies; the filing of information returns by non-profit organizations; rules for amateur athletes; trust arrangements and, finally, regulations permitting supplementary pension plans to be treated as retirement compensation arrangements.
Government Orders
To conclude, the tax measures which were announced in the February 1992 budget, including those before us today, form a key and integral part of the action plan of the government to implement an economic agenda supported by Canadians in every part of the country. This plan includes action to bolster economic activity by cutting personal income taxes, action to boost the housing industry through the home buyer's plan and action to encourage productive investment that will create jobs and provide for incentives to the manufacturing and processing sector, to provide further incentives for R and D and to provide and improve investment instruments and facilities so that more people can invest in productive enterprises that will create jobs and create wealth.
This bill gives legislative effect to measures that will directly benefit Canadians and to strengthen the economic recovery now under way. As well, we are moving second reading of the bill at this time to give taxpayers and their advisers the assurance of the government's commitment to these measures. I think that is a very important signal.
With these measures in mind and in the interests of all Canadians, I hope and I urge that all members of the House will support this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and speak on this bill, Bill C-92, which as you can see is an extremely complex and thick piece of legislation. It has an awful lot of technical changes and an awful lot of provisions in it, many of which, by the way, we support. We think there are many good things in this bill.
The problem we have is with the complexity of the bill, the length of the bill and with the innumerable measures. I have to be very honest with you, Mr. Speaker, it is very much a question of trust. When you look at a bill like this and you realize the vast implications of some of these measures, you have to wonder if you trust this government to be telling you absolutely everything up front? I have to be very honest and say to you that I know the Canadian people have lost a lot of their faith and trust. As a result of that, they are not sure they want to support all of these initiatives, as I am not sure that I want to support all of these initiatives. If I had a lot of faith, perhaps I would.

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
I also would like to remind the people sitting in this House today that in 1982 when a Liberal government introduced a complex bill such as this, the then Conservative opposition filibustered. If you recall, Mr. Speaker, the bells rang for a full two weeks in this House because they felt they could not support one bill dealing with that many complex issues. At that point the bill was split up into a number of more digestible parts.
I want to remind this government of this. It took such drastic measures to ensure that things were dealt with in a clear and open manner, insisted upon it and for that matter paralysed this House for a full two weeks. As one of the finance critics I follow those bills more closely than I do some of the others. I am sure the government is doing it with many of the other bills we see before this House.
The government continually brings in a whole mishmash, a whole host of measures, some of them extremely complex. Some of the bills we support whole-heartedly. However, there are others which the government is trying to sneak in so it can say to the people of Canada: "We offered them what they wanted but they voted against it". We honestly have to oppose the things we think are wrong.
It has been a method of this government to continually bring in a number of measures which would not be supported by the majority of Canadians and to include them in a bill, perhaps such as this one, that a number of Canadians would support.
I say to the people of Canada there are many things in this bill that I personally support but I want many more explanations before I will whole-heartedly support it. I am sure there are many things in it that I would not support were I to know expressly what they meant in the long run.
Therefore, I will be forced not to support this bill. I think it is a question of absolute honesty and ensuring that all details included in this package are absolutely transparent and for the good of all Canadians.
Some of the measures included in this bill are things we ourselves had been pushing this government to bring forward. I remind all Canadians that we had been asking
for quite a while that Canadians be allowed to use their RRSPs to purchase homes. That measure of course is included in this particular bill. That is something we believe in and which has been brought forward. It has helped. It has caused some stimulus, perhaps not as much as we would have liked it to.
We believe that the recession has been such that some of these measures were not as efficient as they might have been had the recession not been so deep, had people not been quite so worried about whether they would have jobs tomorrow. Therefore they have put off buying homes. In that particular instance I hope the date is extended so people can use their RRSPs to purchase their first home.
When it comes to reductions in the individual surtax from 5 per cent to 3 per cent I really do believe this government was honestly trying to give Canadians a break. One of the things this government fails to take into consideration whenever it brings in such a measure is the fact that more often than not other levels of government move in and take over the vacated place.
Over the last years this government has consistently reduced transfer payments to the provinces and the provinces are also in a terrible cash crunch. In the case of Ontario no sooner had this reduction been announced than the NDP government moved in and took it over.
In effect Canadians have not had a break-at least the people in Ontario and I cannot speak for other provinces but I would suspect it is pretty well happening in other areas. Ontario took up the slack and absolutely moved in and that is the end of the benefit to the people in Ontario. I was wondering if there were other provinces that did the same thing.
British Columbia.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
British Columbia is doing the same thing.
While we have the Minister of Finance before us I would like to determine whether there is any way before bringing in measures such as this that he could work in tandem with the provinces to ensure that the benefits flow to those intended to receive them.
February 23, 1993

It is absolutely important when we bring forward such a measure that we know it will actually happen. This is not happening. It is true that our coffers will lose that much but the provincial coffers will take it up. It is not to say the provinces do not need the money. I am sure they do, as we do for that matter.
We are all battling the deficit. Perhaps we should have kept the tax room instead of giving it to the provinces. That is a consideration when realizing that they move in right away. It is extremely difficult to negotiate with the provinces. I understand that. Somewhere, somehow we have to get our act together. When we do something at one level we have to ensure it is supported by other levels of government.
I am going to get off base just slightly here because I like these figures. I realize the NDP has just come out with its policy on replacing the GST. One of the things it said was that it would increase the tax on wealthy Canadians.
I notice that Canadians who would have the reduction in the surtax over a five-year period would have had a saving of $6.6 billion. What that says to me is if the surtax is increased by 2 per cent, the supposed windfall a tax on wealthy Canadians would bring in is perhaps not as large as might be necessary to replace the GST.
If this is something that would bring about a cost, in this case of $6.6 billion and if it is reinstated, then it would stand to reason that the only moneys found would be $6.6 billion approximately over the next five years. The GST net is now bringing in close to $16 billion and that is only for one year.
$15.4 billion.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
It was $15.4 billion for 1991-92. I just want to remind the NDP there is a very wide gap between what it has said and what it has to replace. It is very important that people realize this.
One of the other measures the NDP talked about was that it would bring back an inheritance tax. I am not sure if I have my figures correct but I know the United States has these kinds of taxes. The population of the United States is much bigger than ours and its wealth tax or inheritance tax brings in approximately $500 million a year. If I am not mistaken that is about the sum total it brings in.
Government Orders
I want to again remind the NDP that the odds of bringing in a vast amount of money from an inheritance tax are not there. One of the reasons it was stopped was that the cost of collecting it was far greater than what actually came in, especially when the capital gains tax was brought in.
In essence, that is a tax on wealth. I am not saying that an inheritance tax would not bring in some money. It certainly would. The amount would certainly not be of the magnitude of $15.4 billion, absolutely not. Therefore we would have to look even further to bring in that kind of revenue in one year.
One of the things that happens when an inheritance tax or a wealth tax is brought in is that a lot of jobs are created for estate planners. If the NDP members are friends with the estate planners and lawyers then they should feel free to bring in all of these estate taxes. They would be their friends for a long time.
I do not believe that is exactly what the NDP members had in mind. I think what they had in mind was to bring in a tax which would bring in some revenues.
I am going through these things because it is very important to realize there has to be a reasoned assessment of how much cash will be brought in. That is because we do have a debt and as Canadians we have to be responsible for tackling that debt.
Another thing the NDP has said is that as a first step it would close loopholes. That of course would bring in billions of dollars. I do not know how much it would bring in. I really cannot say.
I have to give some credit to the Conservatives. As much as it pains me I do. They also have been trying to close loopholes. As soon as a new tax change comes into play lawyers and accountants quickly find a way around it. It is almost a whole industry and it is difficult to control. We absolutely have to continue to close those loopholes.
On the other hand, I do not believe that $15.4 billion in taxation will be found after closing those loopholes. I may be wrong but I would be very surprised if that happened. As a matter of fact if revenues of that size were involved in closing loopholes I have a feeling that this cash-strapped government would have found a way of getting a hold of those moneys by now.

Government Orders
As much as they like big business and trans-nationals, I think they are also concerned with our debt, at least this is what they say. I have to believe that this is true because it is something we all face together.
I digressed a little bit because but I thought it was essential to explain this.
I also believe that the NDP plan touched upon the 21-year rule on family trusts. I must thank the minister for explaining the 21-year rule and for making it so clear that there are really no vast amounts of money hidden.
I have seen some of the householders which have been sent around. I have one here which gives an example of a trust of about $70 million established for someone in 1969. Today that trust would have a value of over $600 million. If it had been kept in very conservative investments such as Canada Savings Bonds then it would have gone completely tax-free for those years. This was in a mail out one of the NDP members sent out to the riding. I have to say that is false. Obviously the minister explained that trusts pay taxes so let us not mislead the Canadian public. Trusts do pay taxes.
We are trying to get at the capital gains. Capital gains happen to either a piece of property or for example shares in a corporation that one may hold for 20 years. Obviously that piece of property or those shares may have appreciated in value.
For example, a house is bought for $20,000. Ten years later the house is worth $200,000 and 15 years later it may be worth $150,000. No taxes are paid on that until the house is actually sold and it is not taxable if it is your principal residence. However, you could own an apartment building somewhere and it would appreciate in value that much. Obviously you would not be taxed on the increase in value until that asset was disposed of.
The same thing happens with trusts. The question I have on trusts is as to why we are extending the 21-year rule. That is not clear in my mind. If I trusted more perhaps I would believe it is simply to allow for some trusts to look after disabled individuals for example, but there has to be more to this than meets the eye.
I know if we had not announced that we were extending the 21-year rule these trusts would have been split up and dispersed. There would have been no capital gains taxation by the way because capital gains are not
paid on a trust when the assets are disbursed to the beneficiaries. It is as if they had held them and had owned the stocks the whole time.
The only time capital gains comes into play on these properties is when the beneficiaries die or if the assets are left in that trust. At the end of 21 years then obviously the capital gains would come into play. Knowing the people who would have charge of these trusts, I do not think they would want to pay the taxes. Therefore, had we not extended the 21 year rule, these trusts would have been distributed to the beneficiaries. A few would have sat on the assets and insisted on paying the capital gains taxes.
I have worked enough in the field to say that nobody likes to pay taxes. Whether you are rich or poor, you will do your utmost to ensure that you plan ahead so you do not have to pay these taxes.
Why are we extending the 21 years? I realize it is an arbitrary number. Somehow I am not clear on why we are doing it. I really wonder if it has to do with control.
I want answers to those questions and I will ask them in committee. I have very grave reservations about why we would leave it. It has been opened up for an extended time, until the last beneficiary dies which could perhaps be another 40 years. Why are we doing this?
Again I remind the House that if the trust is distributed to the beneficiaries and they live another 40 years, they do not pay capital gains on it for the next 40 years, or until they sell or die. I think it is very important to make it absolutely clear that these things must be understood. You can really mislead people into believing there are vast amounts of tax dollars we are not tapping. There are not, unless the government is keeping things from us, which it may well be doing. I have already said that it is a question of trust.
That is an unfortunate statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
I have to agree that it is an unfortunate statement, Mr. Speaker. However, there is an unfortunate state of affairs in this country. We no longer trust what is happening in our parliamentary institutions and I do not trust the government. I am an elected MP, here to represent my people and I worry about sleight of hand. I am worried because of the complexity of some things.
February 23, 1993

Why are all these measures in one bill? Why wait so long after the budget was presented to actually bring this bill forward? I have to wonder if it is in the hopes that we will forget what it contains and will be so busy with other things that we will just pass it without asking questions. There is no hope of that.
I will outline some other things which are included in this bill that we should be considering, such as the expansion of the definition of marriage for income tax purposes to include common law relationships. I think we should expand that definition. However, we have no way of knowing really if it is going to happen or not. We are saying to Canadians: "You can now file as married and we trust that you will". I trust that many will. However many will not because they may not even be aware of the changes in the legislation for one thing. I am of the opinion that the legislation may not be definitive enough about how it will be applied. Again, these are questions that I will have to clarify.
There are measures that will assist Canadians with disabilities. I think that is a very laudable endeavour and we should assist Canadians with disabilities.
The reduction of the manufacturing corporate income tax rate is a good idea. Our industries have been decimated. They need all the help they can get. I hope that the provincial governments will not come in and undo whatever measures we have brought forward at this level. In this way we hope to help the manufacturing sector compete and be able to expand its base and operations because we absolutely, desperately need the jobs in this country. The healthier our manufacturing base is the better it is for us.
One of the other measures that really irritates me is the disallowance of the capital gains exemption on capital gains accrued after 1992 on real estate held for investment purposes. There will no longer be that $100,000 capital gains which could be used against this particular kind of purchase.
A person investing in foreign bonds or foreign shares will be able to use the $100,000 capital gains exemption on the sale of them. We should ensure that the moneys we allow under that $100,000 capital gains be investments made solely and completely here in Canada. This particular policy should not penalize Canadians who are
Government Orders
investing locally and purchasing an apartment building or something of that nature versus someone who is investing offshore. It is absolutely essential that we continue to encourage Canadians to invest in Canada in every way we can.
I hope when we go through this bill that some amendments can be made to ensure that Canadians invest their money here. It is the only way we can ensure a viable corporate infrastructure. If we do not invest in our own companies and ventures, how can we expect others to invest in Canadian ventures? It is essential that this be looked into.
The reinstitution of the small business development bond program is certainly a good idea and I support that initiative. We wonder what form this government will continue to take. There are so many technical changes in this particular bill that I am forever worried about it. All you have to do is read any one page and even the explanations. The Minister of Finance said to read the explanations and I would like to read some to you. They are very complex.
This is just one and it concerns the trusts. "Every trust shall on each of the following days be deemed to have disposed of each property of the trust that was capital property other than depreciable property, or land included in the inventory of the trust for proceeds equal to its fair market value on that day and to have reacquired the property immediately thereafter for an amount equal to the fair market value and for the purposes of this act those days-".
It goes on. It is written in very small text and it is extremely complex.
One of the other measures in here also deals with trust. The government is stating it will tighten up the rules so one trust cannot transfer assets to another trust.
I want to ask something that is very important to me. I was under the impression that now, before this legislation is passed, trusts could not dispose of an asset by transferring it to another trust without incurring capital gains. Perhaps this is a loophole it is closing but I was under the impression this was not possible and any kind of transfer of asset would call the deemed realization. It would be as if it were sold, capital gains would come into play and it would be taxed.

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
Not only are trusts taxed but the trusts that are set up by someone who is alive, that is not an estate trust, are taxed.
Any incomes they have are taxed at the top rates. They do not have the graduated rates. Only estate taxes would be taxed at the graduated rates. That is where a trust was set up at the behest of someone who has passed away.
I am extremely anxious to go through this bill and ensure that everything being said to us is really included in it. It is going to a very long and difficult process. I worry that it is going to be rushed as with everything else that happens in this House. We wait and wait to introduce a bill and then we bring in closure. We say "we absolutely have to have this bill today. We cannot go five minutes past this time". Even though it was introduced in the February budget and here we are at the end of February 1993, a full year later, this government will come and say: "Rush, rush, rush, we have to have it".
Again it is a question of trust. Why would the government wait so long to introduce a bill such as this if it contains only good things? It would not even have to worry about rushing people if the bill is as good as it is reported to be.
The government could and I am sure members of a committee would be quite happy to facilitate the discussion and hurry the bill through if it is as good as it says it is.
The government waits and waits. The first reading of this bill was on November 26,1992 and the changes were introduced in the budget of February, 1992. The government will say we did not sit during the referendum.
We could have sat during the referendum. There was nothing preventing us from sitting here in the House of Commons, one, two or three days a week. Perhaps we could not have sat full time but we certainly could have spent more time looking after the affairs of the nation during the referendum campaign. The opposition would have been willing to spend some time in the House of Commons during that time. Of course we do not say what happens in this House. That is always in the hands of the governing party. In this case it is in the hands of the Conservative government.
Why did we wait so long? Please do not bring in closure. Do not rush this bill through committee. Just
recently I had the opportunity of sitting on a committee where exactly the same thing happened. Rush, rush, rush, we had to have this bill out of committee within two days. There was next to no time to hear witnesses. We had to cut back on everything because we were in a big rush and had to hurry up and get the bill through. The government wanted to bring in closure and ram everything through because, as the government says, it controls everything.
If this bill is the bill the government says it is, then do not rush it through. We should be given the time to really study some of the clauses in here so we will know exactly what the effects of them are.
At times there are many things we wonder about. We wonder whether we should be going ahead with some of these tax cuts in light of what has happened with the provincial governments. Maybe we should question that. It may be too late but these are things we really have to consider. We cannot act independently as if we live in a vacuum here in Ottawa. Many things happen across the country while we stand here deliberating or sit here listening.
We must work in tandem. I say this over and over again. I have worked as an accountant most of my life and have been involved in the financial aspects of many organizations, including municipal governments. I have always been very conscious that debt is a bad thing. When I was at the municipal level I helped bring in some policies which really enhanced the position of our municipality. These kinds of problems are really near and dear to my heart, but I insist that this level of government stop behaving as if it were the only one.
Recently this government announced it would freeze grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities. The municipalities really count on these grants in lieu of taxes. The government is going to freeze them to the same rate as they were in 1992.
Mr. Speaker, if you are sitting here by yourself and not worrying about what happens around you, you might say: "Well, it is not so bad. You know, it would not be that bad. I mean, we are cutting back expenditures", but municipalities are facing not only cutbacks from the federal government, but cutbacks at the provincial level. The municipalities have nowhere else to go. A taxpayer is a taxpayer. He or she is a Canadian.
February 23, 1993

We can cut back and say: "Look at the good job we've done managing our debt". Meanwhile the municipalities are burdened with these excessive taxes and responsibilities which many of them are going to find more and more difficult to meet. Have we then done our best for the people of Canada?
I would say to you, Mr. Speaker, we have not. We must work in tandem with all other levels. I cannot stop talking about what has happened in Ontario and British Columbia and will continue to happen probably in other provinces. As soon as we give one group a tax cut which it asked for and desperately needs, another level moves in. If we cut back on transfer payments then the province has no choice but to cut back to the municipalities or cut spending.
Ontario obviously has not cut spending despite the allegations of the treasurer of Ontario that its deficit would be under $10 billion for the year. I am saying deficit. That is only for one year, ladies and gentlemen. A deficit is the amount spent over and above what is raised in taxes.
I read just recently that the province of Ontario is looking at a deficit in the neighbourhood of $13.9 billion. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, shame. I think it is absolutely a horrendous amount of debt to add to the already heavily burdened people of Ontario and Canada because everyone pays, not only the people of Ontario. It affects the economy across the country.
I know the government consults with a lot of people from single interest groups. They say: "I want, give me and let go of the other ones". The government should consult not only with these single interest groups, because we must consult with everyone, but with all Canadians and other levels of government to ensure that whatever is brought forward in the next budget we do not have the kind of scenario that is happening now.
The debt is the debt of all Canadians, whether it is held at the federal, provincial or municipal level. One may say: "Well, municipalities are not allowed to run deficits". No, they are not, but they do borrow for capital projects. Many municipalities have borrowed quite heavily for municipal capital projects. I think it is important to remember that.
Government Orders
We can no longer afford to behave as if we are one level and the others do not count. We have to sit down together and work together to solve this economic crisis.
I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for being so patient with me. I will say to you in ending that I wish it were different. I wish I could trust this government and believe everything it is saying, but I must respond and say this government has lost the faith of all Canadians. Therefore I cannot support this piece of legislation at this point.

Mr. Speaker, we were just treated to a delightful rendition of what is wrong with the Liberal Party as far as trying to figure out where it stands on things. The member who just spoke with respect to the private family trust tax changes began by praising the minister for making it absolutely clear that what the NDP had said about these tax changes was not true. She then went on to say that she did not trust the government and that she had some doubts herself about whether this was an appropriate change to this legislation.
Whatever your position, if you are with the government you had something there that you could take from the Liberals and run with; if you are suspicious of the government and do not trust these changes, you also had something that you could go with. This, of course, is characteristic of what we see time and again from the Liberal Party when it comes to this issue as well as many other issues. I am thinking particularly of this but there are many other examples such as the North America free trade agreement and the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, and the need to abrogate the one and not get into the other.
Bill C-92 is a bill about tax changes. I would like to speak to what is in the bill. I want to concentrate first on the whole question of the changes to the tax laws affecting trusts. Changes to the legislation concerning the taxation of private family trusts were first proposed by the Minister of Finance in draft legislation on February 11, 1991. Despite considerable criticism from the professional community, these changes were then included in draft legislation of technical amendments, released in December 1991. The legislation was introduced into the House by notice of a Ways and Means motion on June 19, 1992.

Government Orders
Current legislation covering private family trusts goes back 21 years to the 1972 tax reform when the federal estate tax was eliminated and the capital gains tax was introduced. This change left a potentially enormous tax loophole. Capital gains taxes are levied only when gains are realized, usually when a property is sold or at the time of death. Because trusts never die, this meant that private family trusts could entirely escape paying taxes on assets held within the trust. So the Liberal government introduced a 21-year rule which required that private family trusts would be assessed capital gains after 21 years and pay tax on their increase in wealth. Income tax is, of course, paid by the beneficiaries when property is distributed to them from the trust.
No capital gains tax has ever been levied under this 21-year rule. All private family trusts which existed on or before 1972 would be subject to tax for the first time in January 1993.
The government is now proposing to essentially eliminate the 21-year rule. Trusts would be allowed to defer the 21-year rule until all the exempt beneficiaries have died. An exempt beneficiary can include a child, spouse or parent of the trust settler, but not any individual of generations subsequent to that of the child. This means that a trust set up for a young child today could go tax free until that child died, which could be 80 years from now. It means that the billions that are presently sheltered in private family trusts will not have to be subject to tax until the last exempt beneficiary dies.
This constitutes a tax loss of billions of dollars. While trusts will be allowed to accumulate wealth tax free for many more decades, the government will be deprived of those revenues to reduce the debt and the deficit.
What are private family trusts? One thing on which I would agree with the Liberal member who spoke earlier is that there is a great deal of confusion and uncertainty about this whole issue and that it is sometimes difficult to understand. I would like to take the House through it in so far as I can and explain how I understand this issue.
What are private family trusts? A private family trust is a legal instrument used to pass on assets to the beneficiaries of the trust who are often the spouses, children or grandchildren. Even a simple private trust I am told costs
thousands to set up. I would not know because I do not know anybody who has one.
How much in assets are held in private family trusts? There is almost no public information available about the amount of wealth held in private trusts. Tkx privacy laws prevent Revenue Canada from providing information about any single trust, and this is probably as it should be. It also does not provide any information about the aggregate amount of assets held in private trusts.
This would certainly be useful information for the public and for Parliament in particular when we are trying to debate this kind of issue. We do not really know the amount of money that we are talking about.
Sources in the financial industry have estimated the total value of assets held in such trusts at $70 billion. This estimate seems fairly reasonable as it represents only 3 per cent of the $2.4 trillion in total assets held by persons and unincorporated businesses in Canada.
The member before me referred to NDP householders that cited this $70 billion. We are certainly not suggesting that there is $70 billion in revenue to be garnered by the government. The $70 billion figure is, as I have said, an estimate of how much money is tied up in these trusts.
What are some examples of private family trusts? Again, we are not really able to say because tax privacy laws prevent information being released about any individual trust. I am told that court records show the trust established for instance by Mr. Bronfman for his daughter had a value of $70 million in 1969.
That is the trust that is referred to in the literature that was quoted by the hon. member previous which would have a value of over $600 million if it had been kept in veiy conservative investment since then.
How much tax revenue will the government lose from this change? With so little information available, it is difficult to estimate just how much tax revenue the government will lose. A very cautious estimate demonstrates what potential revenue is at stake.
If only 1 per cent of the $70 billion in trusts was subject to tax next year, a marginal tax of 30 per cent would raise over $200 million. That is not to be sneezed at, especially when times are tough.
February 23, 1993

What do trust tax professionals say about this change? "There is no question that it represents a massive windfall for existing trusts." This is from Sydney Goldstein of Goldstein and Goldstein, Ottawa.
Another quote from Katherine Bush of Blake Cassels: "A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential political supporters also should be listed as a reason for the draft legislation".
From Neil Brooks, the Associate Dean of Osgoode Hall Law School: "The government has given Canada's wealthiest families notice that it intends to give them a gift worth several billion dollars".
From Arthur Drache of Fraser and Beatty: "If legislation now before Parliament is not passed before the end of the year, thousands of trusts could be hit with massive tax bills".
Why is the government proposing this change? The government argues that these changes are necessary for a number of reasons. First, it has argued that the existing 21-year rule might interfere with trusts established by parents for the benefit of their disabled children.
Exploitation of the needs of disabled children is immensely cynical and makes little sense in this context. Anyone structuring a trust for a disabled child would design it so that the child had an ongoing income and not a lump sum payable at some point in the future as would be the case with most of the trusts affected by the 21-year rule.
As tax lawyers Sydney Goldstein and Katherine Bush have argued, if the government was really concerned about the needs of disabled kids a better solution would have been to declare a special exemption for the disabled. This argument about the disabled is just so much political cover with the government grasping at some compassionate looking straw in order to justify what it is doing for other reasons.
Second, the government has argued that unless the rules were changed some trusts may not be able to pay the taxes without the selling of assets, perhaps including a controlling block of shares in a private company.
This argument has some validity but it still falls short of the mark, it seems to me. Private trusts have had a full 21 years to plan for this tax, much more than ordinary taxpayers get. Besides, taxpayers in this situation could
Government Orders
still utilize the $500,000 small business capital gains exemption to avoid selling assets.
The government says it is closing a loophole with this bill by preventing rollovers from one trust to another. It is true that a clause in this bill does close a potential loophole and we support this, but it does not mean that the government is justified in creating another massive loophole. There are other ways that this could have been dealt with.
Why was the 21-year rule set at 21 years, you might ask? The period of 21 years was apparently chosen in order to be consistent with trust tax law and to be consistent with the then current age of majority.
Will not application of the 21-year rule be hard on widows who do not have funds to pay tax, for instance, on income producing real estate held in a trust? Although it may be onerous for the beneficiaries of some trusts to pay taxes in one shot after 21 years on their capital gains, there is a provision to pay taxes from a 21-year deemed disposition in up to 10 annual instalments in subsection 159(7) and 159(6.1) of the act. This will provide some relief for trust beneficiaries with modest incomes who do not wish to dispose of the asset at this time.
Again, I repeat, it is not uncommon for Canadians of all walks of life to experience difficulty in paying their taxes. Why this particular difficulty should be addressed when the difficulty of so many ordinary Canadians in paying their taxes is not taken into consideration at all is what mystifies us.
Twenty-one years is an arbitrary amount of time. Do these changes not make trust tax more consistent with the taxation of capital gains which is only collected upon disposal or death of recipient? People mig'ht ask this question about our position on this legislation.
It is true that the 21-year rule is an unsatisfactory and relatively arbitrary rule which is inconsistent with taxation of capital gains and was probably designed to fail. It is not hard to imagine that when the Liberals brought this in in 1972, they at the same time figured that at some point the very people who were concerned at that time would bring concerns to them in the future and have this changed. If the aim is to make trust tax more consistent with capital gains tax then realized capital gains should be taxed when the trust settler dies as well as when the last beneficiary dies. However, such a change would eliminate many of the tax advantages of setting up family trusts.

Government Orders
In addition and perhaps more important, all the substantive changes which affect the taxation of private family wealth have allowed substantial tax breaks because they have not been retroactive. Change may be needed to improve poor legislation, but why have the transitions resulting from the changes always allowed big tax breaks by grandfathering?
Financial officials argue that there will be no revenue loss because if these changes do not go through, most trusts will dispose of their assets through rollovers or other mechanisms to avoid the tax anyway. Is this true? This is a hypothetical argument because these measures may or may not be easily available depending on the type of trust, but just because there are avoidance mechanisms does not mean that the government itself should roll over and play dead by opening up a big loophole.
Instead, the government should use the anti-avoidance provisions of the tax act or act to close these loopholes. It is not enough to simply argue that these people will find other ways not to pay taxes. That may be an unfortunate truth about our tax system, that a certain class of people will always find a way not to pay their taxes and that lawyers will always find ways to exploit whatever changes are made. However it has more to do with original sin than it has to do with tax law and has more to do with lawyers than it has to do with tax law. Surely the government could find some way to address these problems without simply conceding defeat in the manner in which it has in this particular bill.
Financial officials say that trusts are not used to avoid tax because in many instances there are measures that individuals can take outside setting up trusts to only pay capital gains taxes when an asset is sold or upon death of the owner and therefore avoid the 21-year rule. How valid is this argument?
Trusts provide many advantages that these other mechanisms could not provide. If the 21-year rule is so onerous and inequitable compared to other mechanisms, why would thousands of people who have set up trusts since 1972 and before these changes were proposed, if the existence of the 21-year rule presents such a tax disadvantage? This argument defies common sense and the logic of our experience with this particular provision.
I hope the hon. member in the Liberal Party had an opportunity to listen to what I said. Perhaps I have
helped to clarify the situation for her. For all these reasons the NDP has tried consciously to bring attention to bear on this particular change. We think it points out the basic moral flaw in the government's approach to deficit reduction, that not all Canadians are being asked to bear the burden of deficit reduction equally and that some Canadians have a special access to the government, that they have the ear of the government with respect to their particular tax problems.
In this case we see that those who have had a concern about the 21-year tax rule have successfully gained the ear of the government and have had this exemption extended by virtue of the legislation we now have before us in the form of Bill C-92.
We take offence at that because we think this simply illustrates the larger picture of how this government has proceeded with respect to tax reform. Tory tax reform has meant more taxes for ordinary working Canadians, for low and middle income Canadians, and has meant special breaks for big business and for wealthy individuals. This particular measure we are debating today says that louder than any other particular measure this government has taken.
I would like to speak to some of the other elements in the bill. One thing that struck me, again talking about the capital gains tax but in another context, is the elimination of the $100,000 capital gains tax exemption with respect to real estate and leaving it in place for equity investments.
We are not in favour of the $100,000 capital gains tax exemption in any event, except of course with respect to the question of principal residences. We continue to favour the larger capital gains tax exemption with respect to the sale of farms, for instance.
However, there may be a way in which a lot of ordinary Canadians have been blind-sided by this particular change. It is not something that I think there is a particular policy on within the NDP, and I have not heard anybody else raise it for that matter. For a lot of working Canadians that I know the only other investment they have in their lives apart from their principal residences may be their summer homes, their cottages at the lake, and this particular bill subjects the sale of their cottages to a capital gains tax.
February 23, 1993

I wonder whether that is what the government really intended. I know that it has received a great deal of mail on it from cottagers and it has not seen fit to change the bill. It strikes me as unfair within the larger context of our tax system.
If we are not going to treat all capital gains equally and if we are to leave equity investments alone so that people can invest in business, make money and not have it subject to capital gains at the same time as dinging a whole lot of ordinary working folk whose only other investment in life might be their summer cottage, there is an inequity that ought to be addressed either by trying to treat all capital gains more equally and not making exemptions which create injustices by leaving some things taxed while other things are not, or by considering this one particular problem a lot of people have and finding a way to give a tax break to people who are not speculating in recreational real estate.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I rise a point of order. Due to the length of time the first two speakers for the other parties had, I wonder if might beg the indulgence of the House to have a few more minutes to finish my remarks.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to extend the time of the hon. member?
Mr. Speaker, we have no objections to giving a few more minutes to the hon. member. However we would not want that to be seen as an indefinite time. I am sure he gets the message.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Some minutes for the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, of course you realize that when the time is extended it is indefinite, but I will not take advantage of the House. I just have a few more things I want to say.
I want to finish up my point about the way in which the particular capital gains tax change in this bill affects a lot of people in my riding, for instance those who have cottages and who are very concerned about it. When we
Government Orders
stack that up against the break the government is giving to people with these large trusts it is pretty hard to defend and I have no intention of defending it.
There is another thing I feel I must respond to. The member from the Liberal Party, obviously not wanting to take too much time to elucidate Liberal Party policy on these matters because there tends never to be any, spent a lot of time attacking the NDP. It seems only just, in the course of natural justice, that I should be able to respond to our accusers.
The member did something which I think is typical of people who have been critical of our over-all approach to tax reform and deficit reduction, particularly when it comes to eliminating the GST, and that is to pick one thing we have listed as a total package that should be brought in to replace the GST and say: "This is not going to replace the $15.4 billion or $15.6 billion that the GST brings in".
The Liberals do not like to talk about the GST, except in the context of the NDP, because they do not have a policy for how to replace the GST. They had one for about 48 hours when they were considering the business transfer tax and a tax on groceries, but that has been deep-sixed. Now we are just supposed to wait until a Liberal government is elected and there will be consultations. Then we will find out what will replace the GST.
We have come forward with a plan for replacing the GST and it is a multifaceted plan. As the member rightly recognized, no one measure is going to replace all that money. But when we consider a number of loopholes that could be closed and the economic growth that could be generated by the elimination of the GST and by other measures to stimulate employment and therefore raise revenues and take people off welfare and UIC, when we consider the expense the GST is to the government both in terms of the cost of collecting and the money the government pays in GST, it all adds up. We believe it is sufficient, along with some of the other tax changes we have proposed, to cover the cost of eliminating the GST.
I have raised a couple of things in the House time and again that I can never get any answer to. In fact whenever I raise these things it is as if I am in the Bermuda Triangle of Parliament. I asked the Minister of

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
Finance a question about a specific tax loophole and he answers a question I have not even asked. I cannot get him even to acknowledge the content or the substance of my question. This happened to me just last week after President Clinton had made his statement with respect to tax reform and I asked the Minister of Finance if he would consider eliminating or reducing the business entertainment tax deduction. Many times before I asked him to do so and he or his predecessor has always risen and said that we have to stay competitive with the United States, that we cannot do that.
Now that the United States is looking at eliminating that particular exemption, I thought this might be an opportunity for the Minister of Finance to reflect on whether or not Canada could now move in this direction and collect some of that $1.1 billion forgone in revenue every year as a result of that particular tax loophole.
What did the minister do? He got up and said: "I know what the NDP wants to do. It wants to get rid of the $100,000 capital gains tax exemption for small businesses". Does this have anything to do with what I asked, anything at all to do with what I asked? Absolutely nothing.
I guess we know our place. The Minister of Finance stays and listens to the Liberals respond to his speech but when members of the NDP get up he takes off. The Liberal member said all those nice things about the Minister of Finance and how he cleared up all the misgivings about the trust tax exemption. It is no wonder he stayed to listen. He probably felt good. He did not expect to feel so good when NDPers got up.
There are ways in which the GST could be eliminated. We have laid them out in a paper we are making available to Canadian people. We would finally like to have a policy debate in this country, not just speculation about who is who in the polls. We would like to have a debate on just exactly what are some of the possible solutions to our problems.
With that, I will not abuse the good will of the House any more and I thank hon. members for their attention.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heard many things during that speech but one thing struck me and I want to know exactly where the NDP stands on it.
The member spoke about how their party was against the $100,000 capital gains exemption being given to Canadians but then he said that he really wanted the capital gains exemption to be in place for people who own cottages. Now that it is being cancelled he would like it to stay in place, because in the past if one owned a cottage and sold it one could use up some of the $100,000 capital gains exemption. This particular piece of legislation closes that loophole.
I thought I overheard the member say that he really wanted the $100,000 capital gains exemption in place. Does that mean that he really approves of the $100,000 capital gains exemption, or what? I would like that clarified because in my mind the NDP has not been in favour of the $100,000 capital gains exemption. I believe it was in favour of the $500,000 capital gains exemption on sale of family farms and those kinds of things, but I did not think it was in favour of the $100,000 capital gains exemption. I wonder if he would clarify that point for me.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite glad to answer that question. One of the peculiarities of the rules of the House-perhaps it is something we should look at, at some point-is that the first speakers for the government and the Official Opposition do not get questioned on their remarks but we get questioned. We welcome the questioning because we like to make clear what we are saying.
I am sorry the hon. member misunderstood me. The point I was trying to make was that what the government has done with respect to the $100,000 capital gains tax exemption was take a measure which we were critical of, as she rightly pointed out, and make it in some senses more unjust.
It has changed it from a policy we object to in principle to a policy we object to in practice because it is so selective with respect to who benefits from it and who does not.
Traditionally, we have been more in favour of capital gains taxes than any other party in this House. That is not a secret. We have always been willing to make exemptions where we thought it was just. Certainly the exemptions we always defended had to do with the family farm and principal residences.
February 23, 1993

I am asking the government to consider, as I am asking others who have policies with respect to capital gains tax, whether or not the blind siding of the family cottage in this recent change is against the spirit of the kind of exemptions the NDP has always defended when it comes to family property.
Maybe that cannot be done. I do not know. In the context of what is now exempt and what is not, it strikes me as unfair that people have to pay that kind of tax on the family cottage when people who are making equity investments and other things the government regards as economically productive do not have to pay that kind of tax.
As with so many other things let us have a system which treats everything equally as much as possible. If we are to get down to picking and choosing what is exempt and what is not, I am simply saying that when we consider what is exempt, including family cottages strikes a lot of Canadians as unfair. I cannot blame them for seeing it that way.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the previous speaker a serious question. I cannot believe what I heard could possibly be the truth. I want to seek clarification.
I understand by listening to the hon. member that back in 1977 the Liberal government of the day introduced legislation to give a special tax break to the wealthiest families of Canada. The assumption was that not paying taxes would allow them to make other investments and therefore help other folks indirectly. It is commonly known as the trickle-down theory or what I like to call the tinkle-on theory.
That was introduced by the Liberals. For years and years the wealthiest families in Canada were able to benefit from it. This is what I am hearing. This tax provision was to expire in 1993, but the present government has decided this should not be stopped now. This incredibly lucrative tax gift loophole to the wealthiest should be extended for a period of time.
The government wants to extend it until the person in whose name the family trust is arranged dies or, in other words, for an entire generation for the wealthiest people of the country. I am sure people listening to this debate cannot believe this is accurate.
Government Orders
I want to ask my hon. friend who obviously has studied this bill carefully and knows the provision we are discussing if this is actually true. Have the Liberals, followed by the Conservatives created the ultimate crass tax loophole where the only beneficiaries will be the very wealthiest people of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it is true. The hon. member for Kamloops points out that there has been a certain kind of collaboration between the Liberals and Conservatives on this issue as there often is when it comes to legislation or policies which benefit the corporate elite in this country, either institutionally or individually. At a certain point there is very little difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives. There may be a kind of feigned difference from time to time for electoral purposes, particularly when it comes to the Liberal Party. It likes to sit a little to the left of centre prior to election time to help give the impression of being an alternative to the Conservatives. But when push comes to shove on the free trade agreement, NAFTA, the trust tax exemption and a variety of other issues there is no difference. The record speaks for itself.
To those Canadians who find the extension of this 21-year rule offensive, not once was the existence of this exemption and the legislation to extend it raised in the House of Commons by a Liberal member. Not once did this matter cross the lips of a Liberal member until today when the legislation was before us almost as a fait accompli. Even then the member who spoke praised the Conservative Minister of Finance for clearing up all the misleading information that the NDP has allegedly been spreading in its householders about this particular legislation.
What more could we ask for in terms of helping us understand who is who, and on whose side particular parties are in this country? It was clear today when there was this sort of-I am trying to think of a polite way to describe the relationship between the Liberal member and the Minister of Finance-cosy mutual admiration society when it came to putting down the NDP version of what is going on here.
I can tell you what is really going on. The Liberals and Conservatives, and not for the first time in Canadian history are once again joining forces to make sure the people with money who really run this country are looked after.

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
