Mr. Speaker, in rising today to speak on second reading of Bill C-92 I have to begin by saying this bill, as presented by the government is an example of how the Conservatives approach governing and the public process. They do so in a way that can only create cynicism and distrust for themselves and, unfortunately, for large parts of that process itself.
If you look at this massive bill you can see that within it are measures that can justify a large degree of public support and I am going to talk about some of them. But there are other measures, the 21-year trust rule in particular, for which the government has not made a case and for which one cannot in my view make the same arguments for public support.
In the Liberal emergency program for economic renewal that we announced in January, 1992 the Liberals called for a change in the law so people could use their RRSP funds toward down payments for homes. The obvious purpose was to encourage the building of more homes and help give a kick-start to the economy. For that purpose we also called for the allowing of a lower down payment for homes.
In this emergency economic renewal program the Liberals called for the creation of an immediate major national infrastructure program. The federal government, together with the provinces and municipalities would provide funds to enable our towns and cities across this country to immediately begin thousands of projects of renewal of national and local infrastructure to improve sewage, water and pollution control systems, roads and bridges. The projects would repair and improve the fabric of our country as a way of contributing to the improvement of our over-all competitiveness while at the same time put thousands of people back to work.
In the budget of February 1992 we saw that the government had accepted some of these Liberal proposals. It said it would ask Parliament to amend the law to allow the expenditure of RRSP funds toward the purchase of new homes, thereby encouraging a renewal of active home building in this country. The budget statement also said the government would allow the lowering of down payments for homes.
Other things we had proposed in our emergency economic renewal program should have been in that budget but unfortunately were not. The budget did not include a national infrastructure program. If that program had been set out in the budget of February 1992 it would be well under way by now. Tens of thousands more people would be working than is the case today, on projects of renewal of infrastucture in towns and cities across this country. Thousands more people would be working to produce the raw materials and equipment needed to carry out these projects of community works and infrastructure renewal.
This has not happened because the government absolutely refused to include in its budget of February 1992 the kind of national infrastructure program and national community works programs we called for in the emergency economic renewal program we announced in January 1992.
In the December economic statement the government adopted some of the language but unfortunately not the substance of the kind of infrastructure program called for by Liberals in their economic program of January 1992. Liberals talked about it back in 1988 in their election platform.
In the December economic statement the government talked about bringing forward certain projects that had been discussed for many months previously, programs that might have been undertaken earlier but about which nothing had been done such as the expansion of Pearson airport. Another example is the upgrading and renewal of highways in Atlantic Canada and in particular New Brunswick.
The other day we saw an announcement by the Minister of Transport that runways would be extended and added at Pearson airport. However, there is no date for the commencement of that work. More startling still, there is no indication of where the funds would come from to enable that expansion of runways at Pearson airport to be carried out.
When it comes to the very necessary renewal of highways in New Brunswick, as far as I can recall there still has not been any final agreement to move forward on this project. There has been no final agreement by the Conservative government to provide adequate financial support to the provincial government of Premier McKenna. When it comes to the projects talked about in the December economic statement, as far as I am aware
February 23, 1993

not one of these projects has actually gotten under way in the sense that there are shovels in the ground, cement being poured and more people working.
If, even in December, the government had adopted the Liberal program of community works, by now many of these projects I have talked about that communities have on the shelf across this country would be under way with people working. Instead they are condemned by the Conservatives to nothing more than the unemployment line, the welfare line and the bread line. Our towns and cities across this country have thousands of projects on the shelf which have been developed and have had environmental reviews, but cannot be proceeded with because they do not have the funds. If we had had a community-based program, as I have already said, then there would have been people working, projects would have gone ahead and the recovery from this Conservative induced recession would be a lot further along a lot more vigorous and a lot stronger than is now the case for many months to come.
The government, in this bill, is trying to implement some tax cuts it talked about in the budget statement, but these tax cuts are extremely modest to say the least. That is why, in replying to the February budget, I talked about these tax cuts being such that the Minister of Finance could be described as two-buck Maz for all they amounted to for the ordinary citizen in this country.
These tax cuts do not even begin to offset the more than 36 tax increases put into effect by this Conservative government since it took office in 1984.
We know that the average middle income family has been hit by close to $2,000 in tax increases by this Conservative government since 1984. By the way, to the extent that there are some very modest tax reductions in the February budget that this bill is supposed to put into place, these have likely been largely wiped out by provincial tax increases unfortunately. These tax increases have been caused by the cutbacks such as the capping of transfer payments by this Conservative government to the provinces and the cutbacks in amounts that would otherwise go to maintaining adequate standards of education, medical care, health care and other basic provincial services.
This Conservative government, in offloading its responsibilities to the provinces, has caused them to either cut back in services or increase their own taxes, or both, in a way that is certainly unfair to average Canadians but
Government Orders
can be attributed in terms of blame directly on to the shoulders of this Conservative government.
One of the proposals in Bill C-92 is to extend the rule with respect to certain trusts and the exemption of the assets in these trusts from capital gains tax, which was a rule that was initially to be in place for 21 years.
If one studies the history of this measure in Bill C-92,1 think one will see something very questionable and suspicious about the way this government has proceeded. This measure, the extension of the 21-year rule, was not in the budget of February 1992 that this Bill C-92 is supposed to implement.
The measure instead was announced by itself in a press release that came out in February 1991 that at that time received very little attention. As I have said, it was not mentioned in the February 1992 budget but it is found in this Bill C-92 which is supposed to be for the purpose of implementing this February budget. It is presented in a way that buries it behind the many other measures in this Bill C-92. Some of these I have been talking about and deserve a measure of support.
When one looks at the press release that the government issued at the time it tabled the Ways and Means motion, which is the basis for this Bill C-92, one will see something rather peculiar. This press release, entitled: "The Explanatory Note for the Notice of Ways and Means motion" talks in brief about the terms of the budget measures which the Ways and Means motion includes and says that it is for the purpose of implementing the budget of February 25, 1992. It then goes on to say that the Notice of Ways and Means Motion also includes a large number of income tax measures: "primarily of a technical nature which were released to the public in draft form on December 20, 1991 and in a number of other releases over the last year". Presumably, in this case, this refers to 1992.
There is no reference whatsoever to this complex and potentially far-reaching proposal to extend beyond the initial 21-year period the special rule regarding the taxation for capital gains purposes of the assets in certain kinds of trusts.
Why was this was not mentioned? What is the government trying to hide here? It did not refer to this proposal in the budget, it did not refer to it in the press release describing the Ways and Means motion. This proposal that was first mentioned in a separate release in

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
February 1991, turns up in this Bill C-92 hidden behind dozens of other measures.
If this trust proposal had been in the budget, I submit that it would have received a lot more attention and scrutiny. If this measure had been in that budget-I am talking about the budget of February 1992-the government would have been obliged to set out information on the revenue effects of extending this rule.
The Minister of Finance has not in the press release of February 1991 or in the notice accompanying the Ways and Means motion and not even in his speech today, if I am not mistaken, given any information whatsoever about how much revenue the government would obtain from taxing the assets in these family trusts if the 21-year rule is not extended. No information is been provided about how much revenue is being lost to the government by extending beyond the 21-year period these special provisions for family trusts.
Surely this is a basic, fundamental and necessary piece of information in order for Parliament and Canadians generally to make up their minds on whether this measure is in the public interest. In the absence of that information, I do not see how this measure can be supported by this House.
We tried to get this information directly from the Department of Finance. It could not or would not give it to us. As I said, by not having it in the budget, it was not set out as was the information about the tax implications of all the changes in the February 1992 budget.
Why has the government not done this? What does it have to hide? Does the government expect us to believe that it did not consider this aspect, that it did not work it out in deciding whether or not to proceed with this measure? The information is there for the public to look at, although sometimes it is hard to obtain. It is there on all the other proposals in this bill but it is missing when it comes to the extension of the exemption for capital gains purposes of assets in these family trusts.
Why is this? The government is certainly giving the appearance of trying to hide something. It gives the appearance of trying to sneak something through and avoid full and proper scrutiny.
The government is not acting in a way which deserves the trust and confidence of this House or the Canadian people. We need to know the tax implications of this measure. As I have said, without it I do not see how this measure can be supported.
The government has not made the case it must make in order to command the support of the House for this measure. That is so even though it is contained in a very large omnibus bill that may have in it other proposals that deserve to one degree or another the support of this House and the public.
By proceeding in this way this Conservative government has tainted all of Bill C-92. We are talking about a basic question of fairness to people who have not been able to avail themselves of these family trust provisions, to ordinary taxpayers who have had their taxes raised some 36 times since this Conservative government has come to office, to unemployed people who are having their unemployment insurance benefits and their eligibility for these benefits cut by this Conservative government and to Canadians who are not getting the levels of services from their provincial governments they deserve because of cutbacks in transfer payments to the provinces by this Conservative government. On the basis of fairness the government should have given us answers and it has not done so.
We have heard also about the changes in the capital gains exemption in this bill. The government has not explained why it has changed this exemption so that people have to pay capital gains tax on their cottages, but others who are able to trade and make capital gains on foreign stocks or bonds still have that full $100,000 exemption.
I say again that this government is proceeding with Bill C-92 in a way that invites cynicism and suspicion. Certainly on that basis I do not see-whatever else there may be in it that is worthy of support-how the bill as a whole can be supported. What we need more than anything else is an election to have a new and better government for this country. I say that it will be a Liberal government.
February 23, 1993

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my colleague on his remarks concerning Bill C-92.
I honestly believe that he is absolutely right that Canadians no longer believe that this government is always being open and fair in its information insofar as it will tell us or disclose exactly what it is doing.
We tend to be faced with a large amount of what I like to call bafflegab or creative accounting in some instances that leads us all to worry and to feel as if somehow there has been a sleight of hand and that we have no idea really what is going on.
Many of the provisions of this act would obviously hurt certain ordinary Canadians. As my colleague mentioned the removal of the capital gains exemption on family cottages. For many people that is perhaps the total amount of their savings. When they sell this they can no longer claim that first $100,000. It is hitting a lot of average Canadians.
Let us be fair. Most wealthy Canadians have had the opportunity to claim that $100,000 exemption already. This particular kind of clause does not affect the wealthy Canadians. It affects the average family groups and Canadians who may have a cottage that they have held in the family for maybe 20 or 30 years and it will cost them dearly. On the other hand, others may be able to apply for this exemption. Perhaps my hon. colleague would like to add to this.
Furthermore, I made the point that this government must start co-operating with other levels of government and not just act as if it is in a vacuum and the problems that are faced here are not faced at other levels. Perhaps the hon. member would like to add to these particular points.

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. colleague has made some very useful points. The government operates in such a way that even when it says it wants to help the ordinary person, it ends up by giving the ordinary person the back of its hand.
I do not think that ordinary people who wanted to see the wealthy bear a fair share of the tax burden expected that in responding to this concern they would find the government saying that they had to pay capital gains on the family cottage. At the same time they did not expect to see large family trusts under the guise of being dealt
Government Orders
with more fairly being put in a situation by the government whereby it is quite possible that amounts that otherwise should be liable to tax would not have to face tax.
As I have said, even when this government claims to be operating in a way that restores a greater degree of fairness to the system, when you get beneath the surface it is found not to be doing that at all.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest as always to the speech by my hon. friend from Windsor. I want to ask a question of the hon. member, who was presumably intimately involved in 1977 when this provision in the tax law was first introduced, the 21-year exemption. I direct this question very seriously. I am not trying to make a political question out of this, but a serious fact finding mission.
I stand to be corrected, but it is my understanding that when this provision was introduced it allowed wealthy families to place money in trust that would not be taxed until the 21-year period had expired. I would call it a 21-year tax loophole or tax break for, again, some of the wealthiest families in Canada. They would be the obvious ones who would take advantage of this.
Is it what I say it is? If so, how does my hon. friend say it was justified at the time? It seems to me to be such a boondoggle but there must have been some serious logic behind it when it was introduced in 1977.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I cannot assist my hon. friend to the extent he would like because I was not a member of the cabinet in 1977 and I was not as closely connected to the subject as I might otherwise have been.
The issue we have to deal with is what do we do now? Whatever justification there may have been for an initial 21-year period, I submit the government has not made the case it should have for its extension. I presume that those people who availed themselves of this 21-year rule did so with the expectation that at the end of that period the tax would apply. Again, as I said, the government has not made the case I think it should have.
I think the issue today is what we do in light of the expiry of the initial provision. I only repeat that the government has not made the case it should have in order to deal with something which could have quite far-reaching consequences.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Windsor for his contribution to this debate. It seems to me that from an historical perspective as he alluded, we have to go back to the Carter royal commission that the Liberal government set up in the 1960s when they tried to treat a dollar as a dollar. Part and parcel of that was giving some people a chance to adjust to this concept.
Of course there were tremendous battles against the Conservatives in the late 1960s and early 1970s to make taxation more fair and perhaps giving a lenient period of time for a number of families to adjust to the new taxation system. As my hon. friend has pointed out very appropriately, we have now reached the point where families with large amounts of money have had an opportunity to adjust. The time has come now to make capital gains a part of the over-all taxation system.
I would like to ask the member from his experience in opposition and in government to perhaps comment on the concept of a dollar is a dollar for taxation. There are a number of issues facing us as Canadians with the high rates of taxation. It seems to me that in the discussions we had on the child benefits package, the government was quite delighted to point out the fairness of targeting people and to make sure that only those in need received it. On the other hand we have this quiet piece of legislation which the Official Opposition has been very vociferous about and very determined. The government has backed away from this principle of allowing taxable dollars to flow into the system appropriately and to be taxed as it is for other families. I think we have to keep our eye on this particular issue to ensure there is tax fairness for everyone.
I wonder if the member could comment on tax fairness for families nowadays.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague has opened a subject about which one could speak at great length in ways I am not sure you would permit.
When we look at the tax system and tax reform, a basic concept we have to keep in mind is fairness. Here we are talking about fairness as between families who were able to avail themselves of these trust positions and those who did not or were not able to do so.
In that context we are talking about something which is a form of estate or wealth tax, the deemed capital gains tax on death. As members of the House know, under our tax law, when somebody passes away it is considered in that tax law as if all that person's capital assets had been sold as of the date of death at fair market value thereby creating a tax liability. So even though that property in fact had not been sold and even though the deceased person's estate may not have the liquid assets within it to pay the tax, it thereby requires the property to be sold in ways that might cause some degree of hardship for the heirs.
Therefore I think we have to bear in mind, with this deemed capital gains tax on death already in existence, what the acceptance of the government's proposal will mean as between those who have availed themselves of extensive family trust provisions and those who have not or are not able to do so. A basic issue as with all aspects of taxation is the issue of fairness.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I sat here today doing duty, as most members have to do once a week, I had some thoughts on some of the information that has been given by the other side.
I felt I would take a few minutes and try to set the record straight on some of the information presented that has implied that this government since 1984 to the present has really not done anything in order to change Canadian taxation.
I would like to start off with a comment that was made by the previous speaker in regard to infrastructure.
Prior to coming to Ottawa in 19821 had the opportunity to be a municipal councillor in a community of about 2,000, involved in an industrial commission for a number of years and the Chamber of Commerce. With an election upon us this year I find it interesting to hear that through the wisdom of our friends from the other side they will cause the infrastructure problems of Canada to be reborn.
I find that quite interesting because if we go back in history to the time when they were sitting on this side of the House, they were the party at the time that cancelled the tripartite position between municipalities, provinces and the federal government.
February 23, 1993

If we go back over time we see some of the ways they tried to generate or stimulate the economy in the early 1980s. Industrial parks were built. The money that was put into these parks was supposed to stimulate industries and create diversification in the economy across this land.
You can see now why we are sitting with the deficit that we have in this country. Those parks that were set up with those dollars spent on infrastructure are still sitting there. The only thing they have today is 10-years worth of growth of trees and shrubs and grass.
That is one reason why each Canadian today is paying for the deficit and misspending of this previous regime over the last number of years. I can tell you that that is the type of spending that Canadians are not interested in.
I wish that the Liberal Party would be straightforward with Canadians. It should really try to tell us where it is going to get the hundreds of millions of dollars that are out there that it wants to put into infrastructure. I believe if municipalities and provinces want to set their priorities and their priorities are infrastructure, then it certainly should be part of the priorities they are setting out and setting some of their other concerns off to one side.
I just want to put on the record today some of the pieces of legislation that we have been able to put forward working with both the previous Minister of Finance and the finance minister today and working with our colleagues. When we got started in 1984, while much of the deficit reduction initiatives had been taken on the expenditure side, over two-thirds of the improvement in the operating budget between 1984 and 1991 was due to program expenditure restraints.
All tax bases have increased in order to bring the revenue and spending into line. Over-all federal government taxes have increased from 16 per cent of GDP in 1984 to 17.6 per cent in 1993.
I would like to just take a few minutes and go through some of the specific tax increases and the areas to deal with. On the personal tax side there is movement to partial indexing, imposition of a general surtax, imposition of an additional surtax on high income earners,
Government Orders
elimination of federal tax reduction and an increase revenue from 6.6 per cent of GDP in 1984 to 8.2 per cent in 1993.
On the corporate side, there are revenues from base broadening under tax reform greater than the cost of rate reductions, imposition of a new large corporations tax raising an additional billion dollars annually, paid by large corporations regardless of their profit position. Revenues have declined from 2 per cent of GDP in 1984 to 1.3 per cent in 1993 due to lower corporate profits.
With regard to sales and excise tax, increases in the manufacturers' sales tax rates prior to the revenue neutral switch to GST, net revenues collected from GST by law must go directly to the public debt and ultimately to reducing the debt.
Let me just take a moment to say how important that is. We have a tendency in governments whereby individuals like to hide if they have the opportunity. Let us hope that in a very few months this same management that is in place today will continue. One of our greatest concerns with the tax that was raised through the GST, in the sum of roughly speaking $15 billion, some other party in power could come in and act like a bunch of drunken soldiers. Rather than taking this money and putting it against the debt, it could end up spending it in areas where I do not believe taxpayers want to see their dollars spent at the present time.
The other part, Mr. Speaker, I should tell you about is changing from the manufacturers' sales tax to the GST. We hear that the Liberal Party is going to scrap the tax. Very good, it is nice to hear. What are they going to do? Are they going to go back to the manufacturers' sales tax?
Let me tell you this, Mr. Speaker, as someone who has come out of the industrial hardware industry where I had to rely on either importing or exporting products. From the manufacturer's side of it and the opportunity and enhancement that has taken place since the start of the GST, it has certainly been able to give our competitors outside of the country a much more severe period of time in order to invest in products that are constructed here in Canada. For our exporters it certainly has increased and figures will show where the increase affects exporting of manufactured goods has certainly been a benefit to Canadians.

February 23, 1993
Government Orders
On the other side of it, I think Canadians are fed up with dealing with the old federal sales tax where a government on budget day can come in and say: "We are going to increase the federal tax by 1 per cent. Thank you very much". In the first two days after a budget people say: "Well, there they go again" and then they have a tendency to forget about it.
Doing it this way with a tax that is shown, Canadians have an opportunity to see whether or not the government manages the tax dollars the way it should. I think the vast majority of Canadians still may not be happy with the GST, but at least they know what they are dealing with. From the other side, all we can hear is: "Give me two years after I am elected and maybe I will see what I can do".
Whether we are talking about companies or whether we are talking about individuals, I do not think Canadians want that uncertainty.
I remember a number of years ago when we were in opposition. We were talking about the fact that maybe it was a time for Canadians to look at wage and price controls. Most Canadians will remember that Mr. Stanfield, our leader at the time, mentioned that we would be looking at a six and five wage and price control.
During the election we heard from the other side: "Don't worry, be happy. We would never do anything like that". Going back in history what happened within a very few months of the Liberals being brought back into power? Wage and price controls.
I also remember in 1980 the federal election was fought on gas pricing. The minister at the time from Newfoundland brought in an 18 cent a gallon hike. Furore hit the country. How could they ever think of increasing the price of gasoline by 18 cents? If we go back over history it was not 18 cents they increased it by, it was not 20 cents, it was not 25 cents, but the meter kept running to well over 30 cents.
Members of the party on the other side are going across the country today stating they are going to do something with the GST. What frightens me, my constituents and many Canadians is that we know the track record of the gang on the other side. They will bring in either a hidden tax or a higher tax. Canadians are not prepared to listen to that.
I would like to move on to some of the other areas of increased economic efficiency such as reform of all the tax bases designed to increase economic efficiency, thereby increasing growth and output.
Elimination of sales tax embedded in business inputs and the tax bias which favoured imports improves the ability of Canadian businesses to compete in both domestic and foreign markets.
With respect to corporate tax, elimination of investment tax credits and fast write-offs for specific investments allows for a lower rate of tax which is the best incentive of all. It has led to greater neutrality between different business sectors which allows businesses to make investment decisions based more on market criteria and less on tax considerations.
With respect to personal tax, elimination of tax preferences, conversion of many deductions into credits and lower marginal rates means decisions are guided by market criteria and not the tax system.
With respect to fairness, there is the introduction of an alternative minimum tax to ensure that wealthy individuals pay tax; the introduction of a large corporation tax to ensure that all large corporations pay tax regardless of their profit position; the lowering of tax rates as a result of tax reform; the conversion of many personal income tax deductions into tax credits; and restructuring of the child benefit system;
I heard the hon. member from the other side complaining earlier about the fact that someone who is on pension and bringing in over $120,000 a year should not be taxed. I have a real problem with that. The system should be there to help those in need. That is certainly what we are trying to do in this country: help those who require help. That is the fairness Canadians want to see in this tax system, a system that is going to be fair to those who need the support.
There is also the enhancement of the refundable sales tax credit to Canadians with modest incomes with the introduction of the GST in 1991. My constituents and Canadians in general are certainly not too pleased but they know they have the opportunity of having a cheque from the government on a quarterly basis and they certainly look forward to that. I can say they call my office if the cheque happens not to be there on that given day.
February 23, 1993

However, enhancement and competitiveness is something that has to be dealt with realistically. One of the problems we seem to face on the other side is that competitiveness is something they are not that concerned about. The fact is that they feel as an old government with old policies they want to go back to those days.
It is a competitive changing world out there that we are dealing with today, whether we are talking about the United States, Europe or Asia. This government has been ensuring that the opportunity is going to come through tax reform. Enhancing that competitiveness is the income tax reform, lowering the statutory tax rates to keep in line with the rate reduction in other countries.
The 1992 budget announced reductions in the tax rate of manufacturing and processing profits and raised the depreciation rate of equipment used in manufacturing processing to help the sector readjust.
I want to talk about that for one moment. One of the key factors we are facing in our country is the restructuring of our industries through modernization, upgrading, new technology. Coming from a resource sector in northern Ontario, let me say that we have gone through some very difficult restructuring times.
We must ensure we can be competitive. For example, in the forest industry-my colleague behind me has a very keen interest in the forest industry in his region of British Columbia-it is important when suddenly the purchase of a new debarker machine for a sawmill operation can be considered. That is going to enhance the opportunity to lower the over-all cost of operation.
That is really what this is all about, being able to help individuals but also being able to help the corporate side to ensure there is a profit. Some people in this House believe that profit is a bad word, that a company should not be making profits.
In order to remain sustainable and develop and enhance the opportunities for a single employer, profitability has to be ensured with the opportunity of that profit being put back into the company in buying new equip-
Govemment Orders
ment and enhancing the opportunity of steady employment. This is the very key portion of what we should be looking at.
The other part is encouraging individuals in risk taking by the introduction of lifetime capital gains exemption.
If you happen to be in the agricultural business, if you happen to be in small business, most of those people work seven days a week, 24 hours a day. They are the key factor of the future of our country. Whether there are two, five or 25 employees, whatever it may be, the small individual companies are the heart and soul of the country.
After years of dedicated work those businesses should have the opportunity to gain a capital gains for the number of hours they have worked. A lot of times it is the husband and wife, or a ma and pa operation. They have worked years and raised a family. Then all of sudden they decide either through normal retirement or because of health or whatever that they want to move on and start a new way of life.
A key factor we should be looking at for Canadians is the opportunity for doing what they believe is correct in investing in and for governments investing in small business.
The other part is the introduction of tax credits for labour-sponsored venture capital corporations. We all recognize we can no longer afford to have labour sitting on one side and management on the other and government sitting in another separate area.
These days, it is critical in order to ensure the opportunities for our children and grandchildren that the enhancement of all sectors be working together. Looking around the world it is certainly taking place in other countries. Labour, management and government are sitting down and looking at joint ventures.
Some have been recognized already in northern Ontario and other parts of the country. It is going to be imperative that government, labour and industry look more at this type of co-operation ensuring that there is stability and also the opportunity of ensuring that jobs are going to continue to be enhanced in Canada.

Government Orders
There is the tax assistance to small business. Canada continues to have one of the most preferential tax systems for small business in the industrialized world. In December 1992 the economic fiscal statement included short-term measures to help small business create jobs and create investment.
One of the contentious issues we seem to be facing here on an ongoing basis is that all of a sudden we have made some major adjustments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
My riding of Timiskaming is going through some difficult times. We are facing about 30 per cent unemployment in my area. From those announcements in December until last Friday, I have had one call. The vast majority of people on unemployment are those seeking employment and they are saying: "Well, it is about time".
It is about time that changes were made. This would assure the small business side and those out looking for employment and those who are employed that we can no longer afford paying for people taking holidays in Florida, paying for people to go moose hunting or paying for people who are just tired of what they are doing and want to sit home and receive unemployment.
Unemployment insurance was never intended to fill in when people decided they no longer wanted to work. It is a safety net that is there to help the individual Canadians who need help. That is really what we are trying to do. We are trying to ensure there is a safety net for Canadians who need help.
When a person who has been working for a small business gets up in the morning and decides that he does not really feel like going to work, he is going to quit, thank you very much, the dollars that have been gone to help train that individual always come back on that small business.
It also means that the small business will be very reluctant to hire new people. Perhaps it has had one or two bad experiences. It has hired people, trained them at a cost of thousands of dollars. All of a sudden the guy says: "I don't like it any more. I am gone". That is the message we are getting.
If you look at the small business investment tax, if you look at the RRSP eligibility investment and changes of the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption to small business shares, these helped firms and the public.
I have tried to give members an overview of what the government has tried to do. It is difficult when you are put in the position we were in 1984. You walk in and the cookie jar is empty. You have everybody wondering how you are going to help people.
The only way we are going to continue to have a country that is viable is for Canadians to come together. Nobody likes to pay tax. Nobody wants to pay tax. However everybody in this House today and a vast majority of Canadians are very fortunate. Our lifestyle has been great. If we are going to continue to give a comparable lifestyle to our children and our grandchildren, we must get our house in order.
I really hope that Canadians will question in the next number of months those who are going to be campaigning and offering all these goodies. Exactly how are Canadians going to pay for these goodies? Are they going to slash or are they going to tax? That is the question that Canadians should be asking any candidate who is making promises.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I noticed the hon. member for Timiskaming talked about the unemployment insurance bill more than he talked about this particular income tax bill.
I know the riding that he represents as I was bom and raised in it. I also know of the high unemployment rate that people are suffering there. To be very honest, I do not know too many people who would quit their jobs because they feel like spending the winter in Florida collecting unemployment insurance.
Furthermore, if anyone does that and if the Unemployment Insurance Commission finds out about it, there is an extremely heavy fine right now in place. The fine runs as high as 200 and 300 per cent of whatever money that was paid out.
The money paid out by UI has to be returned over and above the extremely heavy fine. Let us quit trying to make Canadians believe that there are hundreds and thousands of people who are quitting their jobs because they can afford to go south to Florida.
Yes, there are many people who can afford to go to Florida and that is their choice. I do not know that many of them are the ones who are quitting their jobs to go there, certainly not in the riding he represents. There are not a lot of very wealthy Canadians in that particular riding. It had some very tough times over the last 20 years or 30 years. It is not just in the last few years that those people have been having difficulties.
February 23, 1993

On another track, I want to ask the hon. member whether he has considered the fact that the government of which he is a member has decided that ordinary Canadians who purchased a cottage 20 years ago for perhaps very little money, when they sell this cottage they can no longer claim the $100,000 capital gains exemption.
I know that in his riding there are many examples of ordinary Canadians-not wealthy Canadians, although there are wealthy Canadians who own cottages-who have not made a lot of money. They have paid a lot of taxes and continue to pay a lot of taxes.
Those people may have purchased cottages for next to nothing because there are many of them in those regions. I know some people who bought cottages 20 years ago for $400. Now the cottage may be worth $25,000 or $75,000. They will no longer be able to get a capital gains exemption when they sell their cottages. These are people who have not made vast sums of money or profits at any other venture. They have not been able to claim the $100,000 capital gains exemption, whereas wealthy Canadians by and large have already arranged their affairs to take advantage of this $100,000 capital gains exemption.
What does the member tell the people in his riding, those same people who bear the brunt of all taxation? What does he tell them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have many constituents in my riding who have $100,000 cottages so I do not think that is much of a problem.
There are people in my riding with cottages that they bought. Maybe they are second and third generation. Maybe some of them bought them for $8,000 or $12,000 and are very fortunate today that those cottages may be worth $50,000 or $60,000.
They may say: "I do not like paying tax. Maybe I hate paying tax". They also look at the fact that the government does not have too many avenues by which it can afford to tax Canadians. They may not like it, but Canadians also recognize that this government or any government today does not have too many options. One
Government Orders
of the options may be taxing a cottage at $75,000 but the return, it having been bought at $12,000, will still be sufficient. The fact is many cottages in our area are transferred in families.
I think that is a boondoggle. Over all Canadians recognize that the government is in difficulty. Canadians recognize that we can no longer spend for tomorrow. What we are now doing is paying for the errors of the last 25 years.
That is a greater concern of Canadians. They want to make certain that the fiscal management of this country is in shape. They have greater concerns about where we are starting. Whether we are talking about municipalities, school boards, provincial or federal governments, all governments have to start to get their taxation in order. Canadians can see debt that is sitting out there. That is what Canadians are more concerned about. They do not want to pay more tax, but they want to ensure that their children have the same opportunities that have been given to them.

Mr. Speaker, the member from Timiskaming is providing a fantastic set of answers. He is suggesting that the legislation is somehow motivated by a desire to bring down the deficit.
At the heart of the legislation is a massive giveaway which tax experts have estimated is billions of dollars of money that would have been received this year by the federal government if it had not moved as it is moving with this piece of legislation to permit family trusts to continue to be exempt from taxation for years and years into the future.
I have a question for the member on something that does not come from myself but from The Financial Post which is normally quite supportive of the government. On this particular scandalous giveaway of tax moneys the government should be receiving, resulting in other Canadians having to pay more taxes, The Financial Post has been very blunt. It has indicated that there could be substantial sums at stake in allowing trusts to defer capital gains taxes further. "Taxpayers should be told how much revenue is at stake and who will benefit most by allowing trusts to defer capital gains taxes for many years beyond the 21 years presently allowed".

February 23, 1993
I ask the member to stand in the House of Commons and tell us how much money is being lost to the finance department of this country. How much extra taxes will have to be paid by Canadians as a result of the government's legislation in front of us today that will extend for up to 80, 90 and 100 years the period during which family trusts do not have to pay a penny in capital gains tax, regardless of how much extra value the assets they hold accumulate during that timeframe? How much money is the government giving away?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have those figures in my back pocket. I can tell the hon. member that in 1985-86 my colleague from Mississauga chaired the finance committee. We heard from Canadians from coast to coast, from companies and from unions with regard to tax reform. The finance ministers between 1984 and the present have certainly done everything they possibly could to tie up, snag, stop or gag tax evasion, tax adjustments.
I guess I should say that the hon. member was part of the finance committee. I would imagine that somewhere in his briefing notes he has that information.
I believe the department is doing everything it possibly can in looking at ways to get tax dollars from Canadians. I would imagine over that period of time it has certainly looked at that area and at this time is not in favour of moving forward.
Mr. Speaker, could we agree to call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to call it one o'clock?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair until two o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 24(2).
The House took recess at 12.56 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, Ottawa and Quebec have just signed an agreement under which $40 million will be used to promote sustainable development in the agrifood sector.
The agreement will provide financing for a number of programs involving research, technological innovation and training. The minister and member of Parliament for Bellechasse said it was now up to the farmers to submit projects to the regional committees. After all, they were familiar with the problems.
According to Quebec minister Yvon Picotte, the regions would be in charge of the programs, since agricultural conditions vary from region to region. The minister said this was an example of co-operative federalism, with duplication kept to a minimum. Administration was kept to a minimum, to ensure that funds provided under the agreement budget would be spent on the projects submitted by fanners.
Mr. Speaker, that is what Quebec farmers have been calling on the federal and provincial governments to do.

Mr. Speaker, according to a secret Conservative Party document now being circulated to its campaign workers, top strategists are encouraging Tory members of this House to abuse their parliamentary mailing privileges.
Today's Globe and Mail reports that the document reads thus: "Using their mailing privileges means they, the MPs, could be in direct personal contact with all of their voters over the next few months. We still have some time so I would encourage you to encourage your incumbents to do as much as they can now".
What an absolutely disgusting and morally bankrupt use of taxpayers' funds. Mailing privileges are just that, a privilege and not a right for government members for their own personal election campaigns.
February 23, 1993

Canadians are fed up with the despicable antics of this government perpetually lining its pockets at the taxpayers' expense. I am quite confident that the people of Canada will severely punish the Conservative Party for this act of thievery in the coming election.

Mr. Speaker, it is no secret that we have in our country a sinking ship, the Mulroney government.
Aboard the ship sails the first mate, the Deputy Prime Minister who happens to come from Vegreville, Alberta. Coincidentally Vegreville will also be the home of the newest national immigration centre, a huge electoral lifeboat.
The name for this style of politically inspired public policy is called pork barrelling of the worst kind.
Transferring the immigration centres across Canada to Vegreville would reduce face-to-face access by citizens and their advocates to government service and would put in peril through the mail-in approach for applications the safety and security of the immigration system itself. It would uproot the employees and impose undue hardships on their families.
I call on this government to rescind this ill-conceived plan. Public policy should be based on what is right for the citizenry and not what is politically necessary to re-elect the Prime Minister's deputy.

Mr. Speaker, in discussions about implementing the North American free trade agreement I urge this government to insist that the Government of Mexico implement an acceptable environmental green plan so that its future economic development will be in harmony with all that is considered necessary and desirable for the future well-being of the entire North American continent.
In that way Mexico would answer those genuine concerns that are being expressed here and in the United States about the possible undue exploitation of Mexico's people, its resources and its ecology.
The North American free trade agreement offers a greater future for all the participating countries but it must be accompanied by environmental commitments that will ensure proper sustainable development.

Mr. Speaker, the 15-month lockout by Nationair of its workers has been lifted. Members of the Canadian Union of Public Employees are voting as we speak in this House.
The commitment and solidarity of these CUPE members in the face of an employer that is more interested in busting the union than in finding a fair collective agreement is to be admired and applauded.
One has to wonder just how much sooner this labour dispute could have been settled had Nationair not been permitted to use scab labour. Four hundred and fifty flight attendants stood on picket lines and watched as scabs took their jobs.
Months of negotiations and conciliation failed to persuade Nationair that collective bargaining is about fairness not union busting. It is obvious the use of scabs prolonged and embittered this dispute.
The ongoing dispute at the Royal Oak mine in Yellowknife also demonstrates that without a ban on the use of scabs in this country unscrupulous employers will never come to the bargaining table committed to finding a fan-settlement.
The only result from the use of scab labour is a poisoned labour relations climate.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian university and other post-secondary students have been facing some very difficult financial problems in recent years due to the constantly increasing costs which they as students have been experiencing.
Moreover, the opportunities which they traditionally have had to finance their studies through summer employment have diminished due to the economic reces-

February 23, 1993
sion which has impacted on so many countries. Many, if not most students, depend to a significant degree on government guaranteed student loans to finance their studies, loans plus interest which must be repaid after graduation.
Regretfully, however, the maximum amount which can be loaned annually to students has not increased since 1984 despite the huge increase in cost which they have had to incur since that date.
Consequently, I would urge those who are currently reviewing Canada's student aid program to increase significantly the maximum amount which can be loaned to post-secondary students. I would also urge that the 3 per cent administration fee be abolished.
*

Mr. Speaker, in the introduction to the green plan the Prime Minister said: "As Canadians we are the trustees of a unique, beautiful and productive northern land".
Where is that sacred trust now as the government prepares to dilute, dissolve or dismember environmental regulations if they interfere with competitiveness or cut into profits? Where now is the 1990 green plan promise to review and update regulations that did not do enough to protect the environment?
Protecting clean air, water and land is important to Canadians. The environment however is obviously on the chopping block of short term economic gain, blind to the duty we hold to future generations.
This government is showing clearly that it does not understand the message of sustainable development, that conserving our resources is the only way we can have prosperity. It cannot even read the balance sheets of corporations that are saving hundreds of millions of dollars by cutting their use of water, energy and chemicals that they flush down the drain.
The government has put an urgent priority on cutting environmental regulations but no priority on improving them.

["Mr. Speaker, the current government and its Liberal predecessor have created a tax system which favours those of wealth and privilege. For example, the government has decided to extend the most famous of all Liberal tax loophole, the one protecting Canada's most wealthy families who have family trusts.
This means that billions of dollars presently sheltered in private family trusts will not be subject to tax until the last exempted beneficiary dies. A fund set up today for a young child would go tax-free for 70 years or 80 years. In our judgment this is very wrong. This is another case where the Liberals created the loophole and the Tories are now widening it. The Liberals feigning ignorance are now crying foul.
February 23, 1993", 'Unlike the two old time parties, the New Democrats believe Canadians deserve a fair tax system. Our plan should raise revenue for necessary government investment in services without overtaxing working Canadians. It would help to provide proper incentives to stimulate the economy.
Providing a special tax which helps only the wealthiest of families in Canada is wrong. It is time for a fair tax system for all Canadians.']

Mr. Speaker, last night 10 of the fittest members of this House put partisanship aside and accepted a challenge from the pages to compete in a game of basketball.
Although the pages are younger, stronger and in far better physical condition, experience, pride and a desire to win kept the MPs in the game. Indeed, the MPs would have won except that an unnamed member was intimidated by the enthusiastic verbal support given to the pages and he missed two free shots at the closing of the game and it ended in a 38-all tie.
Mr. Speaker, your office has always done an outstanding job selecting young Canadians to serve as pages. Without exception in my memory they have been a credit to themselves and to this House. They are intelligent, articulate and hard working. This year they also appear to be outstanding athletes.
On behalf of all members, I want to indicate what a privilege it is to know them and how satisfying it is to be able to compete athletically and not to lose.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate our friends in Madawaska-Victoria on Unitel's choosing Edmundston as the location for its customer service centre.
I want to thank Bob DeGrace and the task force that prepared the submission of the Chaleur region and the Acadian peninsula and presented it to Unitel.

Purolator, Federal Express, Cameo and now Unitel, another chapter in the New Brunswick success story.
Four hundred new jobs in the telecommunications sector is a tremendous breakthrough and is really a tribute to the competent, highly motivated bilingual work force that is available in northern New Brunswick.
As Bathurst Mayor Ken Frenette said: "All the applicants have learned a lot from the Unitel exercise". The experience we gained will serve us well as we continue to work together to demonstrate that New Brunswick indeed is open for business.
February 23, 1993

Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell you about a development project that will generate 1,000 permanent jobs in my riding. Intrawest Corporation, the largest Canadian resort developer, which owns the Blackcomb ski centre in British Columbia and has owned the Mont-Tremblant ski resort since August 1991, will invest $413 million over the next five years to make the resort into an international four-season tourism centre.
I am pleased to announce to my constituents in Laurentides that this project will create 5,500 full-time jobs during construction, which begins in April, and 1,000 permanent jobs after that.
I close by pointing out the managers' enterprising spirit and the $20 million in government money under the Canada-Quebec tourism development agreement. This project will stimulate the economy in the region and in Laurentides.

Mr. Speaker, the federal government is being something less than honest when it talks about cutting its expenditures, controlling them by cutting back on federal transfers to the provinces. The bulk of these transfers go to post-secondary education, health care and social assistance.
Every one of those programs is important. They are similar from one province to another throughout Canada, although not necessarily equal. These are all very important parts of what it is to be a Canadian, that we have these services available.
The government says that it is saving taxpayers' money when it knows full well that every dollar that is cut back from the provinces has to be raised by the provinces by raising taxes or some other method.
It knows there is not the flexibility there to cut back on expenditures. The federal government in saying this is
called saving the taxpayers' money is being something less than forthcoming.

Mr. Speaker, in the debate yesterday about the fixed link, one of the members in opposition suggested that the construction benefits would all be realized in other countries.
In fact the bridge will be constructed mainly on Prince Edward Island and a staging area will be established at Borden. It will be built in components and floated into place. Construction will be of concrete and by far the majority of labour and materials will go to people in the maritime provinces.
The main benefit will be on completion when the unemployment rate will begin to be equalized with the mainland maritime provinces.
Currently the unemployment rate on the P.E.I. side of the strait is 35 per cent higher than the New Brunswick side. This will change when the bridge is complete, the impediment to trade is eliminated and thousands of new jobs are created.

Mr. Speaker, the city of Nepean condemns the announcement of the Minister of Finance that the Conservative government will no longer recognize the municipal formula for grants in lieu of taxes to Canadian municipalities for municipal services to federal facilities.
The chairman of the RMOC said: "This change in policy not only violates the longstanding federal practice of honouring municipal tax rates, but it also represents intrusion into the municipal domain of setting property tax rates. This action contravenes the fundamental principle of fair and equal taxation treatment for all property owners receiving identical municipal services. The Government of Canada as a property owner proposes to disregard its responsibility for paying its fair share of costs associated with providing municipal services. The result of this action will be to shift the tax burden to other property owners within the municipality".

February 23, 1993
By refusing to adhere to the municipally set rates, this government is clearly demonstrating its dishonesty, its treacherousness and its arrogance. The federal government should pay equal taxes on its properties the same as all other property owners.

Mr. Speaker, the environmental assessment for Pearson International Airport was completed in November 1992 but not released to the public until last week.
Then the minister advised that he was rejecting virtually every recommendation from the environmental review panel. In particular, the environmental review panel suggested a short 4,500-foot runway parallel to runway 33 for small aircraft.
The minister rejected that proposal and is going to build a full runway. The environmental review panel suggested sound-proofing to retrofit residences and schools and other such buildings. The minister rejected that recommendation. Indeed, the minister has refused to compensate anyone or assist anyone for substantial increases in air noise.
There is no point in the Government of Canada financing an environmental review of a project if the Government of Canada is not going to be bound by that review.

Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday of last week an hon. member from the other side rose in this House to praise his government for the success of the Canada Scholarship Program.
In the heat of the moment and possibly overcome by emotion, it seems the hon. member lost sight of some of the facts. He failed to mention that not only will students be forced to pay income tax on their scholarships, but they have been robbed of the six month interest free grace period. That adds six months of additional interest to those financially strapped students who must borrow to access post-secondary education.

To top it all, the hon. member, who was obviously in a state of uncontrollable excitement, forgot to mention that his government had decided to break its promise to
eliminate the 3 per cent tax on student loans in exchange for six months more interest.
The Conservative government will take nearly $60 million from students of modest means.

Will this government stop erecting barriers for students, our young men and women, and start doing something about it now?

Mr. Speaker, scientists say that human activities accelerating the natural greenhouse effect could cause future climatic changes to occur 100 times faster than during the last ice age. We can do something about this by becoming more energy efficient.
This is an environmental citizenship message from Environment Canada. Yesterday was the commencement of the environmental citizenship messages program.
This new green plan program is designed to use Canada's existing network of 60 weather offices and the Canadian Meteorological Centre to deliver daily educational messages on issues like global warming, waste reduction, water conservation and spaces and species to the media and the general public.
I know that Canadians will listen to these messages.

Mr. Speaker, the current government and its Liberal predecessor have created a tax system which favours those of wealth and privilege. For example, the government has decided to extend the most famous of all Liberal tax loophole, the one protecting Canada's most wealthy families who have family trusts.
This means that billions of dollars presently sheltered in private family trusts will not be subject to tax until the last exempted beneficiary dies. A fund set up today for a young child would go tax-free for 70 years or 80 years. In our judgment this is very wrong. This is another case where the Liberals created the loophole and the Tories are now widening it. The Liberals feigning ignorance are now crying foul.
February 23, 1993

Unlike the two old time parties, the New Democrats believe Canadians deserve a fair tax system. Our plan should raise revenue for necessary government investment in services without overtaxing working Canadians. It would help to provide proper incentives to stimulate the economy.
Providing a special tax which helps only the wealthiest of families in Canada is wrong. It is time for a fair tax system for all Canadians.
['Hear, hear.']

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister. We have been informed that the government intends to present the bill on the North American free trade agreement tomorrow, although parallel negotiations with the United States and Mexico are not to begin until next month.
Could the Acting Prime Minister tell the House why they are in such a hurry, when the American government does not intend to proceed with legislation until it has obtained parallel accords on the environment and employment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canada and the United States have begun the legislative process on the parallel accords. We have opportunities to discuss the parallel accords with the Americans and the Mexicans. This process is to begin in mid-March and I think that both processes will proceed at the same time and may not end until the summer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why is the government in such a rush to table a bill that obviously will be amended? In his statement last week the President confirmed to the Congress what Mr. Kantor had said before, that they would not proceed unless they had agreements on manpower and the environment.
Oral Questions
Why would the government like the House of Commons to pass the bill right now when we all know that there will be changes? If there are no changes the Americans will not proceed and we will have lost all our bargaining chips at the table.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend must realize that all three countries have signed the North American free trade agreement. What my hon. friend is talking about is what will be the components of the parallel accords.
The free trade agreement itself will be legislated by all three countries as it was signed last December. There may be some variation in what the different countries would like to see in the parallel accords. That process, as I said, will commence in the middle of March and it will proceed in parallel with the work that is going on in legislating the agreement.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a supplementary question to the minister.
The minister is admitting that there will be some negotiations starting next month. Last week he suggested that we should have a North American environmental commission to deal with the problems of the environment. He realized that there was a change in the position of the Americans because there was a change in the administration in the United States.
In Canada there is a very good chance that before this bill is approved by the Americans there will be a change in government here and that will change the policies.
Would it not be fair, in the fifth year of its mandate, for the government to slow down a bit and wait to see what the Canadian people will decide about the government? If you are elected you will go all the way, but we know that you will not be elected and there will be some major changes to this deal.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the drool coming out of the comers of my hon. friend's mouth is not becoming of him. He is not going to win the next election. He will not have an opportunity, as he says, to renegotiate the agreements.

Oral Questions
As I have said before, what is it that the hon. Leader of the Opposition is going to renegotiate? If you are going to renegotiate you have to give to get. The Americans are looking to see some changes in the supply management system. They are looking for changes in the cultural exemption which we have negotiated.
Which of these is my hon. friend willing to give up, because he has to give if he is going to get.

Mr. Speaker, the United States, as the minister knows, does not hesitate to put forward its values and its ideas in parallel accords.
The three parallel accords to which the minister has referred may not alter the NAFTA text itself but will certainly change the way in which the NAFTA agreement will operate.
Will the Canadian government, not the U.S. government, for its part take this opportunity to propose a parallel accord on subsidies and anti-dumping so as to protect Canadian interests and to prevent the sort of trade harassment that we have suffered from the United States in recent months?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me take my hon. friend back to February of a year ago when it was the Canadian government in the negotiations in Montreal that put forward some specific proposals for trilateral agreements on labour and on the environment. It was the Canadian government that put these forward.
We were not able to get agreement from the other parties at that time, but now that the Americans are coming back and looking more productively at this, it has given us a new opportunity to carry forward the proposals we put forward a year ago.
My hon. friend is asking about the countervail and anti-dumping elements. He knows we have a very good proposal on the table right now in the Uruguay round. I know that he and I are both in agreement in hoping that we will see some successful conclusion of this in a very
short period of time. That I think will provide the answers he is looking for.

Mr. Speaker, the best way for the government to proceed would be to embody the GATT text on subsidies in the North American free trade agreement.
The minister knows that it was his government which took the intellectual property provisions and particularly the drug patent requirements out of the Uruguay round text and put them in the NAFTA.
If that is good policy, why is it not equally good policy for the government to take the subsidies text out of the GAIT and put it in the North American free trade agreement, either in the text itself or in a parallel accord?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in a perfect world I would be inclined to agree with my friend. However, you have to get agreement from the other two parties. The other two parties are saying: "Let us complete it in the Uruguay round". On that basis what is included in the Uruguay round will be included as part of the disciplines the North American free trade partners must follow as well. That is the approach we have decided to follow.

Mr. Speaker, we know where the Conservatives stand on the NAFTA. It would really be helpful to the debate if we found out where the Liberals stood on the NAFTA.
My question is directed to the Minister of Finance who will know-
Oh, oh.
No one cares where you stand. You are irrelevant.

They seem a little bit irritated. I wonder why.
The minister will remember back in 1972 when he sat on this side the Liberal government brought in the family trust loophole to the tax system. He will remember days and days of railing on against this unfair provision.

February 23, 1993

Now that there are probably $70 billion wrapped up in family trusts and now that his government has extended the Liberal program to provide a tax-free holiday for an entire generation, for the wealthiest families of Canada, can he explain if it was wrong back in 1972 how can it be right today in 1993?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should really do his homework on this issue.
What we are doing in the current legislation is indeed closing a loophole which allowed the prevention of taxes being paid on capital gains. That is precisely why this measure will improve that and make it more fair and equitable, as I am sure the hon. member would want us to do.

Mr. Speaker, the fact remains that many people who know what they are talking about have called this a very significant tax break in the millions of dollars for some of Canada's wealthiest families. Yet the Conservatives want to extend this Liberal loophole as they have done with so many other things, just showing the similarity between the Conservatives and the Liberals when it comes to things that affect the very powerful in this country.
I want to go back to a question I asked the Minister of Finance last week which he did not answer. It has to do with the business and entertainment tax deduction, another loophole which many in this country use to finance their box seats at hockey games, Expo games or whatever the case may be.
Previously the Minister of Finance said to me that he could not change it because we had to remain competitive. The Minister of Finance now knows that the Americans are looking at changing it. I asked him in the House last week if he would look at changing it and he did not answer the question.
Will he now answer that question? Will he look at changing that deduction?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member is influenced by what the Americans do, I should ask him whether he is now in favour of a national sales tax, a
Oral Questions
GST or a value added tax which the Americans are considering as well.

Mr. Speaker, you just cannot get the Minister of Finance to answer the question with respect to the business and entertainment tax deductions.
Why do we not try again? The business and entertainment tax deduction, is the government thinking of changing it now that it can do so without harming our competitive position with respect to the United States?
While he is at it, if the Minister of Finance is concerned about loopholes, could he explain to the House why the Canadian government voted against Interfirpol, an organization suggested to deal with the way in which other countries become tax havens and put countries like Canada at a disadvantage? Why did the Government of Canada vote against creation of that?
The hon. member has put his question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member is not a great supporter of the small business community and I know he is not a great supporter of the Canadian Restaurant Association.
Answer the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: He will just have to wait and see what the budget holds.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Yesterday in response to the report that Transport Canada is failing to collect landing fees owed by some air carriers, the President of Air Canada said:
If that is the way the game is played to keep the field level we would like to play it the same way.
Thousands of Canadians in financial difficulty would dearly love to forgo their taxes as well. Why has the government been discriminating among air carriers in the collection of these fees? When did it become government policy to let businesses off the hook for unpaid taxes and fees owing to the Government of Canada?

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the government has never let any airline off the hook in collecting its taxes.
Because the airline industry is a cyclical business, we have from time to time accommodated some airline companies that were experiencing problems. We have accommodated some airlines in other ways. Each airline has been treated fairly.
We will continue to do so by being prudent and at the same time compassionate for the jobs of the thousands of people employed in the airline industry in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, lots of Canadians would like to see some compassion from the government when it comes to collecting taxes.

The minister's policies are in complete disarray. He has reduced them to some vague statements about capacity and about offering financial assistance through the back door. If he is unable to formulate a policy, why does he not table the review panel report that has been on his desk since January 30?

Mr. Speaker, I find it rather difficult to follow the hon. member's logic. Some time ago he worried about what we were going to do to ensure that a major company did not go bankrupt before all these avenues had been explored. We did what was necessary to give the company ample time to examine the situation and I think that so far this has produced satisfactory results.
As for the report by the National Transportation Act Review Panel, it has been submitted to us. We are now examining the report and we intend to table it in the House as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, the minister talks about satisfactory results. But this Minister of Transport is presiding over the disintegration of Canada's airline industry.
The president of Canadian Airlines is asking Ottawa to order reductions in passenger capacity. The president of Air Canada is asking for deferrals in landing fees. The president of Nationair is asking for federal cash assistance from the national government.
The question Canadians are asking is: What is this minister doing? When is this minister going to produce a plan to stabilize, to resurrect, to save the Canadian airline industry from a government-made disaster?

Mr. Speaker, over-all, the airline industry is going through a very difficult period world-wide.
In other countries, for example the United States, many companies have gone bankrupt causing the loss of many jobs in the industry. However, Canada has been able to maintain all the airline companies in a living situation by applying the policy of being compassionate to the people and at the same time being fiscally prudent.
Mr. Speaker, this government's policies are killing our airlines. Unless the minister thinks he is Pontius Pilate will he immediately take all necessary action to prevent a disaster in the industry?
